_comment: Fourteen tours built around the books. A stop is {id, target, record?, title, caption, source, quote?, image?}; record names the Braidense reference entry (ECO.04) of the same book when the stop opens on a copy filmed in the flat; a quote is {text, lang, translation?, attribution, url?} and is verbatim from the source named; an image is {file (under tour-images/), credit, link, alt}, public domain or Creative Commons. Captions never refer to the map, its sources or its process.

tours.title: Behind The Name of the Rose
tours.blurb: Eco's first novel and the books it was made from: the lost book of Aristotle that kills, the Franciscan mystic who became a character, the inquisitor's own manual, the encyclopaedias the monks quote, and the philosophers who lent the detective his name and method.

stops.title: Il nome della rosa (1980)
stops.caption: The novel began, Eco liked to say, with a single image: a monk poisoned while reading a book. A friend at a small publisher had asked him for a short detective story; he answered that his would run to five hundred pages and be set in a medieval monastery, went home and started a list of monks' names. Two years later the book existed.

source.label: The Paris Review, 'Umberto Eco, The Art of Fiction No. 197' (2008)

quote.text: One day in 1978, a friend told me she wanted to oversee the publication of a string of little detective novels written by amateur writers. I said there was no way I could write a detective story, but if I ever did write one it would be a five-hundred-page book with medieval monks as characters.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, interviewed by Lila Azam Zanganeh, The Paris Review, 'The Art of Fiction No. 197' (2008)

stops.title: Postille a Il nome della rosa (1983)
stops.caption: Three years after the novel Eco wrote a short afterword explaining how it was built: why a found manuscript, why the Middle Ages, why a detective, why a labyrinth, and why a title that means too many things to mean anything. It is the best guide to the shelves that follow, since it is Eco himself naming his sources. This is the 1984 Bompiani printing.

source.label: Eco, Postille a Il nome della rosa (1983); in English as the Postscript to The Name of the Rose (1984)

quote.text: In truth, what really happened with my desire to write a book on comedy was that I wrote The Name of the Rose instead. It was one of those cases in which, when you are unable to construct a theory, you narrate a story.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, interviewed by Lila Azam Zanganeh, The Paris Review, 'The Art of Fiction No. 197' (2008)

stops.title: Aristotle, Poetics, in Bernardo Segni's Italian (1551)
stops.caption: The book that kills. The second book of Aristotle's Poetics, on comedy, was lost in antiquity; in the novel it survives in one poisoned copy, and the murders are committed to keep it unread. Eco's own Aristotle is Segni's Florentine translation of 1551, printed with the Rhetoric.

source.label: The Paris Review, 'Umberto Eco, The Art of Fiction No. 197' (2008)

quote.text: When I wrote The Name of the Rose I didn't know, of course, since no one knows, what was written in the lost volume of Aristotle's Poetics, the famous volume on comedy. But somehow, in the process of writing my novel, I discovered it.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, interviewed by Lila Azam Zanganeh, The Paris Review, 'The Art of Fiction No. 197' (2008)

stops.title: Ubertino da Casale, Arbor vitae crucifixae Iesu (Venice, 1485)
stops.caption: A Franciscan mystic of the early fourteenth century, whose Tree of the Crucified Life reads history as a battle between the poor Christ and the Antichrist. In the novel he is the old friend who warns William against the flesh and the inquisitors. Eco owned this incunabulum and counted it among the essentials of his collection.

source.label: Eco and Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2011), the chapter on incunabula

quote.text: I only possess about thirty incunabula, though they do include what you might call the 'essentials'. For instance, the Hypnerotomachia Poliphili, the Nuremberg Chronicle, Ficino's translation of the Corpus Hermeticum, the Arbor Vitae Crucifixae Jesu Christi by Ubertino Da Casale (who became one of the characters in my Name of the Rose).
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco in conversation with Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2009; English translation 2011), 'Every book published today is a post-incunabulum'

stops.title: Bernard Gui, Manuel de l'inquisiteur
stops.caption: The inquisitor who arrives on the fourth day and sends the cellarer to the stake was a real Dominican, Bernard Gui, whose Practica inquisitionis is a working handbook for interrogating heretics. The trial in the novel follows its procedure. Eco's copy is the French edition of the manual.

source.label: The Name of the Rose, fourth and fifth days

stops.title: Roger Bacon, Opus majus (London, 1733)
stops.caption: William of Baskerville calls Roger Bacon his master: the thirteenth-century Franciscan who wrote on optics and lenses and foresaw flying machines, which is why William wears spectacles and expects wonders of natural science. The Opus majus was not printed until 1733, from a Dublin manuscript; this is that first edition.

source.label: Eco, Postscript to The Name of the Rose (1983); the novel, first day

stops.title: William of Ockham, Philosophical writings
stops.caption: The other half of the detective's mind. Ockham's razor, the rule that entities should not be multiplied beyond need, is William's method, and the novel's last line, that we hold only bare names, is Ockham's nominalism in a monk's mouth. A modern selection of his philosophical writings, underlined and annotated in Eco's hand.

source.label: Eco, Postscript to The Name of the Rose (1983)

stops.title: Wittgenstein, Ricerche filosofiche
stops.caption: Not a medieval book at all. Some of the wisest things the monks say are modern, and Eco enjoyed passing off Wittgenstein as a fourteenth-century thought. On the last night of the novel William tells Adso that the order our mind imagines is like a ladder, built to reach something and to be thrown away once climbed, and gives the sentence in medieval German: it is the close of the Tractatus (6.54) in disguise. The ladder allusion concerns the Tractatus, a different work from the Philosophical Investigations shown here.

source.label: Il nome della rosa, 'Settimo giorno, Notte'; Wittgenstein, Tractatus logico-philosophicus, 6.54

quote.text: The order that our mind imagines is like a net, or like a ladder, built to attain something. But afterward you must throw the ladder away, because you discover that, even if it was useful, it was meaningless.
quote.attribution: William of Baskerville in The Name of the Rose, 'Seventh Day: Night', translated by William Weaver (1983)

stops.title: Alain de Lille, Distinctiones dictionum theologicalium (about 1473)
stops.caption: On the first day William quotes Alan of Lille: every creature of the world is like a book and a picture to us, and a mirror. The verse is the whole theory of signs of the novel in one line. Eco's Alan is not the poem but his Distinctiones, a dictionary of the meanings of scriptural words, one of the oldest printed books in the house.

source.label: The Name of the Rose, first day, Prime

stops.title: Isidore of Seville, Etymologiae (Strasbourg, about 1473)
stops.caption: The encyclopaedia of the early Middle Ages, twenty books on everything from grammar to ships, explained through the origins of words. It is where the monks' knowledge of names, beasts and the sciences comes from. Eco's copy is the Strasbourg printing of about 1473, with his own card recording the dealer and the price.

source.label: Nuovo and Coletto, 'Gli incunaboli di Umberto Eco', AIB Studi 62 (2022)

stops.title: Bartholomaeus Anglicus, De proprietatibus rerum (1480)
stops.caption: A Franciscan encyclopaedia of the thirteenth century: God, angels, the body, beasts, stones and herbs, in nineteen books. It is the kind of learning the abbey's herbalist and the painter of marginal monsters draw on. The 1480 printing, among Eco's incunabula.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Il fisiologo (the Physiologus)
stops.caption: The bestiary behind every bestiary. A late-antique book in which the lion, the phoenix and the unicorn each carry a Christian meaning, it is the source of the animal lore the monks trade and of the creatures Adelmo paints in his margins. Eco's copy is Francesco Zambon's Italian edition.

source.label: Eco, Art and Beauty in the Middle Ages (1959; revised 1987), on the symbolic reading of nature

stops.title: Alessandro Manzoni, I promessi sposi
stops.caption: The found-manuscript device that opens the novel, an old text discovered and retold, is Manzoni's opening gambit in The Betrothed, the Italian classic every schoolchild reads. Eco wrote about Manzoni's slow beginning, the long description of the lake of Como before anything happens, as a lesson in how a text teaches its reader the pace it wants.

source.label: The Paris Review, 'Umberto Eco, The Art of Fiction No. 197' (2008)

quote.text: Researchers have run tests on the frequency of words in Manzoni's The Betrothed, the masterpiece of nineteenth-century Italian literature. Manzoni had an absolutely poor vocabulary, devised no innovative metaphors, and used the adjective good a frightening amount of times. But his style is outstanding, pure and simple.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, interviewed by Lila Azam Zanganeh, The Paris Review, 'The Art of Fiction No. 197' (2008)

tours.title: Behind Foucault's Pendulum
tours.blurb: The second novel and the occult library that feeds its Plan: the Hermetica and the scholar who dated them, the magicians and the Rosicrucians, Kircher and Fludd, the Kabbalah, and the Templar and conspiracy literature that three Milan editors weave into a plot the world believes. Almost all of it stands in the rare-book room.

stops.title: Il pendolo di Foucault (1988)
stops.caption: Three editors at a Milan publishing house, bored by the occultists whose manuscripts they read, invent a world conspiracy of their own, and the believers come for them. Eco said the book grew from two images, the pendulum he saw in Paris at twenty and a boy playing a trumpet in a cemetery, and that it took him eight years to find what to put between them.

source.label: Louisiana Channel, 'Umberto Eco: I Was Always Narrating' (2015)

quote.text: One was the one of the pendulum that I saw at the age of 20 in Paris. And, the other was the image of a boy playing the trumpet in the cemetery. That was an event that really happened to me. And, I said: 'Ah, a novel starting with the pendulum and ending with the cemetery - fine'. What to put in between: it took me eight years to discover.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, Louisiana Channel interview 'I Was Always Narrating' (2015)

stops.title: Hermes Trismegistus, Pimander, in Ficino's Latin (1481)
stops.caption: The founding text of the hermetic tradition the novel's Diabolicals live by. Cosimo de' Medici had Marsilio Ficino set Plato aside to translate these Greek dialogues first, believing them older than Moses; for a century Europe read them as the wisdom of ancient Egypt. Eco named this incunabulum among the essentials of his collection.

source.label: Eco and Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2011), the chapter on incunabula

quote.text: Ficino's translation of the Corpus Hermeticum, the Arbor Vitae Crucifixae Jesu Christi by Ubertino Da Casale (who became one of the characters in my Name of the Rose), and so on. My collection is very focused.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco in conversation with Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2009; English translation 2011), 'Every book published today is a post-incunabulum'

stops.title: Isaac Casaubon, De rebus sacris et ecclesiasticis exercitationes (1614)
stops.caption: The narrator's namesake. Asked in the novel whether he is the Casaubon of Middlemarch, he answers that there was also a Renaissance philologist of that name, but no relation. In his 1614 Exercitationes, Casaubon used linguistic and historical evidence to argue that the Hermetic writings belonged to the early centuries CE, not the remote antiquity traditionally attributed to Hermes Trismegistus; the novel's Diabolicals still live by the older belief. Eco explained that he chose the name for the philologist and only later noticed Eliot's character.

source.label: Umberto Eco, 'Between Author and Text', in Interpretation and Overinterpretation, ed. Stefan Collini (Cambridge University Press, 1992)

stops.title: Agrippa, De occulta philosophia (1533)
stops.caption: The Renaissance summa of magic: numbers, planets, angels and talismans in three books, by a wandering German scholar who was also a soldier and a lawyer. Agrippa is one of the authorities the novel's occultists cite, and one of the sources Eco's history of the perfect language follows on the magical power of names. The first complete edition of 1533.

source.label: Eco, The Search for the Perfect Language (1993), on the kabbalistic and magical languages

image.alt: The Theban alphabet from Agrippa's De occulta philosophia (1533)

stops.title: Trithemius, Steganographia (1608)
stops.caption: The abbot of Sponheim's manual for sending secret messages by the spirits of the air, so notorious that it circulated in manuscript for a century before anyone dared print it. Beneath the angels it is a real cipher book. The hidden message Colonel Ardenti brings to the editors is the novel's version of what Trithemius promised.

source.label: Eco, The Search for the Perfect Language (1993), chapter on polygraphies

stops.title: John Dee, Monas hieroglyphica (Antwerp, 1564)
stops.caption: Elizabeth I's mathematician and magus condensed the whole cosmos into one glyph, the monad on this title page, and later took dictation from angels. The novel stages Dee, the angelic conversations and the monad in its Elizabethan chapters of the Plan. Eco's copy is the first edition, kept among the most precious books.

source.label: Eco, The Search for the Perfect Language (1993), chapter 8, 'Dee's Magic Language'

stops.title: Fama Fraternitatis (1615)
stops.caption: The Rosicrucian manifesto: in 1614 an anonymous pamphlet announced that an invisible brotherhood of the Rose Cross was about to reform the world, and half of Europe wrote to join. Nobody answered. The novel spins its Plan out of this text and its sequels; Eco read them as the perfect case of a secret that exists only because people look for it. A 1615 printing, bound with the Confessio.

source.label: Eco, The Search for the Perfect Language (1993), chapter 8

image.credit: Anonymous (attributed circle of Johann Valentin Andreae), 1614
image.alt: Title page of the Fama Fraternitatis (1614)

stops.title: Chymische Hochzeit Christiani Rosencreutz (1616)
stops.caption: The third Rosicrucian text, the Chemical Wedding: an alchemical romance in which Christian Rosenkreutz attends a royal wedding over seven days, full of lions, virgins and a castle of wonders. Its author, Johann Valentin Andreae, later called it a joke. Eco kept it beside the Fama.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

image.alt: Title page of the Chymische Hochzeit Christiani Rosencreutz (1616)

stops.title: Robert Fludd, Utriusque cosmi historia (1619)
stops.caption: The English physician's history of the two worlds, the great cosmos and man the small one, with its engravings of the divine monochord and the universe as a mirror. Fludd is one of the authorities the occultists invoke, and Eco kept his works beside his Kirchers, among what he called the eccentric minds of his collection.

source.label: Eco and Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2011), 'Every book published today is a post-incunabulum'

quote.text: But I also possess the works of Robert Fludd and a fair few other eccentric minds.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco in conversation with Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2009; English translation 2011), 'Every book published today is a post-incunabulum'

stops.title: Athanasius Kircher, Oedipus Aegyptiacus (Rome, 1652 to 1654)
stops.caption: Three folio volumes in which the Jesuit polymath read the hieroglyphs as a secret hermetic wisdom. Every reading is wrong and the whole is magnificently coherent, which is exactly what the Diabolicals do to history. Eco lectured on Kircher's Egypt at the Collège de France with the Sorbonne's Egyptologists in the front row, and told Carrière he owned every Kircher but one, the little Ars Magnesia, a book without pictures that nobody had thought worth keeping.

source.label: Eco and Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2011), the chapter on incunabula

quote.text: I have all his books except the Ars Magnesia, which is impossible to get hold of, despite being a small book with no illustrations. Kircher wasn't yet known at the time of publication, so I expect only a few copies were printed.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco in conversation with Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2009; English translation 2011), 'Every book published today is a post-incunabulum'

image.alt: Mithras slaying the bull, a plate from Kircher's Oedipus Aegyptiacus

stops.title: Athanasius Kircher, Mundus subterraneus (1664)
stops.caption: Kircher's underground world: the fires, rivers and currents he imagined beneath the crust, with the famous plate of the earth's inner furnaces. The telluric currents the Plan sets out to control, with the pendulum as their compass, are the novel's use of this book's physics.

source.label: Foucault's Pendulum, the chapters on the telluric currents and the Umbilicus Mundi

stops.title: Knorr von Rosenroth, Kabbala denudata (1677)
stops.caption: The Latin anthology through which Christian Europe read the Zohar and the doctrine of the ten sefirot. The novel is built on those ten: its parts are named Keter, Hokhmah, Binah and so on down the tree of the sefirot. Eco's set stood on the shelves of his rare-book library.

source.label: Foucault's Pendulum, the ten parts named after the sefirot

image.alt: The tree of the sefirot from the Kabbala denudata

stops.title: Sefer Yetzirah, in Postel's Latin (1552)
stops.caption: The Book of Formation, in which God creates the world by combining the letters of the alphabet. Belbo's word processor is called Abulafia after the medieval kabbalist who permuted those letters to reach ecstasy, and Eco's history of the perfect language opens with this book. The first Latin translation, by Guillaume Postel.

source.label: Eco, The Search for the Perfect Language (1993), chapter 2, 'The Kabbalistic Pansemioticism'

stops.title: Paracelsus, Opera omnia (Geneva, 1658)
stops.caption: The collected medical and alchemical works of the Swiss physician who renamed himself after Celsus and burned Avicenna in public. His doctrine of signatures and his homunculus run through the talk of the novel's occultists and the epigraphs of its chapters.

source.label: Foucault's Pendulum, the epigraphs and the occultists' talk

stops.title: Picatrix, the Latin version
stops.caption: A medieval Arabic handbook of astral magic, translated for Alfonso the Wise, that tells you how to draw down the power of the planets into talismans. In the novel it lends its name to a Milanese occult circle and its magazine. Eco's copy is the Warburg Institute's edition of the Latin text.

source.label: Foucault's Pendulum, the chapters on the Milanese occultists

stops.title: Le tombeau de Jacques Molai (1796)
stops.caption: A pamphlet of 1796 by Cadet de Gassicourt, one of the first to claim that the Templars survived their suppression as a secret society and took their revenge on the French monarchy in the Revolution. The novel takes an epigraph from it: this is the shelf where the Plan's idea was first printed.

source.label: Foucault's Pendulum, chapters 22 and 25

stops.title: Abbé Barruel, Mémoires pour servir à l'histoire du jacobinisme (1799)
stops.caption: A Jesuit's four volumes blaming the French Revolution on a plot of philosophers, Freemasons and Bavarian Illuminati: the grandfather of every conspiracy theory the novel plays with, and a book Eco returned to in The Prague Cemetery. His copy is the Augsburg edition of 1799.

source.label: Foucault's Pendulum; The Prague Cemetery (2010)

stops.title: Nesta Webster, Secret Societies and Subversive Movements (1924)
stops.caption: The English writer who joined the Templars, the Illuminati, the Freemasons and the Protocols into one continuous conspiracy: the twentieth-century template of the Plan. The novel names her in its pages on the Protocols and takes an epigraph from this book. The 1924 first edition.

source.label: Foucault's Pendulum, the chapters on the Protocols

stops.title: Baigent, Leigh and Lincoln, Il Santo Graal
stops.caption: The bestseller of 1982 that made the Priory of Sion and the bloodline of Christ into pseudo-history. The novel takes an epigraph from it, and Casaubon predicts that a book about Rennes-le-Château would sell by the hundred thousand. Twenty years later Dan Brown proved him right, and Eco claimed him as one of his characters.

source.label: The Paris Review, 'Umberto Eco, The Art of Fiction No. 197' (2008)

quote.text: The author, Dan Brown, is a character from Foucault's Pendulum! I invented him. He shares my characters' fascinations - the world conspiracy of Rosicrucians, Masons, and Jesuits. The role of the Knights Templar. The hermetic secret. The principle that everything is connected. I suspect Dan Brown might not even exist.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, interviewed by Lila Azam Zanganeh, The Paris Review, 'The Art of Fiction No. 197' (2008)

stops.title: Frances Yates, Giordano Bruno e la tradizione ermetica
stops.caption: The historian who reconstructed the Renaissance hermetic tradition, from Ficino's Hermes to Bruno's art of memory, and made it respectable to study. The novel's occult genealogy covers the ground she mapped. Eco's copy is the Italian translation.

source.label: Eco, The Limits of Interpretation (1990)

tours.title: Behind The Island of the Day Before
tours.blurb: The third novel is a Baroque library in disguise. Nearly every chapter is titled after a real seventeenth-century book, and its Jesuit, its wit and its swordsman are built from Kircher, Tesauro and Cyrano. This tour goes from the novel to the shelves where those books stand.

stops.title: L'isola del giorno prima (1994)
stops.caption: A young Piedmontese gentleman, shipwrecked in 1643, is stranded on an empty ship within sight of an island that lies across the date line, on the day before. Eco drew the whole ship so as to know where his character could go, and refused to let the plan be printed so that the reader would be as lost as Roberto.

source.label: Louisiana Channel, 'Umberto Eco: I Was Always Narrating' (2015)

quote.text: For 'The Island of the Day Before', I designed all the interior of the ship - very complicated with a staircase, a ladder there... because I had to know how my character could move. But, when the German publisher … wanted to reproduce the design on the book, I said: 'No'. … The reader has to be as confused as the character.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, Louisiana Channel interview 'I Was Always Narrating' (2015)

stops.title: Emanuele Tesauro, Il cannocchiale aristotelico
stops.caption: Chapter 9 of the novel carries this title, and Father Emanuele, who builds an Aristotelian machine for generating metaphors, is modelled on Tesauro, the Turin priest whose Aristotelian Telescope of 1654 is the great treatise of Baroque wit. Eco's copy is the modern edition.

source.label: L'isola del giorno prima, chapter 9, 'Il Cannocchiale Aristotelico'

stops.title: Kenelm Digby, Discours sur la poudre de sympathie (1658)
stops.caption: Chapter 16 takes its title from this book: Digby's lecture at Montpellier on a powder that heals a wound by being applied to the weapon that made it. In the novel a wounded dog is kept aboard so that its bandage, dipped in England at fixed hours, will tell the ship the time at home, and so its longitude. Digby was a real courtier, and the powder was really sold.

source.label: L'isola del giorno prima, chapters 16 and 17

stops.title: Digby, La polvere di simpatia
stops.caption: The same lecture in a modern Italian edition, the version a novelist reads first before hunting down the 1658 printing. Sellerio of Palermo published it in 1989 in its series Il divano.

source.label: University of Bologna, Biblioteca Umberto Eco

stops.title: Jean-Baptiste Morin, Longitudinum nova et hactenus optata scientia (1634)
stops.caption: Chapter 17, 'The Desired Science of Longitudes', is the Italian of this title. Morin proposed finding a ship's position from the moon, one of the schemes the novel's Cardinal Mazarin sends Roberto to sea to spy on. Longitude was the great unsolved problem of the century, and every crank in Europe had an answer. The Paris printing of 1634.

source.label: L'isola del giorno prima, chapter 17

stops.title: Christiaan Huygens, Horologium oscillatorium (1673)
stops.caption: Chapter 15 is called 'Clocks (Some of Them Oscillating)': an echo of Huygens's treatise on the pendulum clock, the clock that promised to solve the longitude problem the novel's characters chase with dogs and powders, and failed at sea. The first edition of 1673.

source.label: L'isola del giorno prima, chapter 15

stops.title: Giovanni Battista Riccioli, Geographiae et hydrographiae reformatae (1672)
stops.caption: Chapter 10, 'Reformed Geography and Hydrography', is the Bologna Jesuit's book on the measure of the earth and seas, first printed in 1661. Its tables of longitudes are the learning Father Caspar brings aboard the Daphne. Eco owned the Venice edition of 1672.

source.label: L'isola del giorno prima, chapter 10

stops.title: Baltasar Gracián, Oracolo manuale e arte di prudenza
stops.caption: Chapter 11 is 'The Art of Prudence', the second half of the title of Gracián's manual of worldly maxims of 1647. Roberto learns the arts of the court from Baroque moralists of exactly this kind. The Italian edition.

source.label: L'isola del giorno prima, chapter 11

stops.title: Athanasius Kircher, Magnes sive de arte magnetica (1643)
stops.caption: Father Caspar Wanderdrossel, the Jesuit Roberto finds hiding on the Daphne, is built from Kircher and his pupil Schott. The novel names Kircher's Ars Magnesia among the readings on cures by sympathy, and dismisses the compass needle as a way to find longitude. This is Kircher's big book on the magnet, in the 1643 edition; Eco owned every Kircher he could find.

source.label: Eco and Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2011), the chapter on incunabula

quote.text: I have all his books except the Ars Magnesia, which is impossible to get hold of, despite being a small book with no illustrations. Kircher wasn't yet known at the time of publication, so I expect only a few copies were printed.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco in conversation with Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2009; English translation 2011), 'Every book published today is a post-incunabulum'

stops.title: Athanasius Kircher, Mundus subterraneus (1664)
stops.caption: Chapter 33 is 'Underground Worlds', the title of Kircher's geology, with its plates of the fires and rivers beneath the crust. The same book feeds the telluric currents of Foucault's Pendulum.

source.label: L'isola del giorno prima, chapter 33

stops.title: Athanasius Kircher, Itinerarium exstaticum (1656)
stops.caption: Chapter 39, the last before the closing 'Colophon', is 'Ecstatic Celestial Itinerary': Kircher's journey through the heavens, in which an angel guides the narrator from planet to planet and shows him that the stars are suns. The Rome first edition of 1656.

source.label: L'isola del giorno prima, chapter 39

stops.title: Thomas Burnet, Telluris theoria sacra (1699)
stops.caption: Chapter 21 keeps the Latin title of Burnet's Sacred Theory of the Earth, the theory that the Flood broke a smooth first world into the mountains and seas we have, and that they are its ruins. Eco's copy is a 1699 edition.

source.label: L'isola del giorno prima, chapter 21

image.alt: Frontispiece of Burnet's Telluris theoria sacra (1681)

stops.title: Giovanni Ferro, Teatro d'imprese (1623)
stops.caption: Chapter 26 is 'Theatre of Devices': Ferro's encyclopaedia of emblems and mottoes of 1623, the language of pictures and words in which Roberto and Father Emanuele court and argue. The first edition, from the shelves of Eco's rare-book library.

source.label: L'isola del giorno prima, chapter 26

stops.title: Pierre-Daniel Huet, Trattato sull'origine dei romanzi
stops.caption: Chapter 28, 'On the Origin of Novels', is Huet's treatise of 1670, the first history of the genre, placed at the point where Roberto begins to write a romance of his own inside the novel. The Italian edition.

source.label: L'isola del giorno prima, chapter 28

stops.title: Fontenelle, Entretiens sur la pluralité des mondes (in the Oeuvres, 1790)
stops.caption: Chapter 34 turns Fontenelle's conversations on the plurality of worlds of 1686 into a monologue: Roberto alone on the ship, reasoning about other inhabited worlds. Eco's Fontenelle is the collected works of 1790.

source.label: L'isola del giorno prima, chapter 34

image.alt: Frontispiece of Fontenelle's Entretiens sur la pluralité des mondes (1686)

stops.title: Gaspar Schott, Technica curiosa (1687)
stops.caption: Chapter 25 keeps the Latin title of Schott's collection of curious machines and air-pump experiments. Schott was Kircher's assistant and the other half of Father Caspar. Eco owned more than a dozen Schott volumes.

source.label: Eco and Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2011), the chapter on incunabula

quote.text: I also have the works of one of Kircher's disciples, another German Jesuit called Gaspar Schott - but listen, I don't want to flaunt all my possessions.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco in conversation with Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2009; English translation 2011), 'Every book published today is a post-incunabulum'

stops.title: Cyrano de Bergerac, Oeuvres diverses (1710)
stops.caption: Roberto's fencing teacher and free-thinking friend Saint-Savin, who dies in a duel at Casale, is usually read as a portrait of Cyrano, the real swordsman and author of a voyage to the moon. Eco owned his works in this 1710 edition.

source.label: L'isola del giorno prima, the Casale chapters

stops.title: Cyrano de Bergerac, L'altro mondo
stops.caption: Cyrano's own voyage to the moon, the free-thinking fantasy that the novel's Saint-Savin talks like: the moon is another earth, the earth another moon, and a philosopher can get there by tying bottles of dew to his belt. The Italian edition.

source.label: L'isola del giorno prima, the Casale chapters

stops.title: Benedetto Bordone, Isolario (1534)
stops.caption: The novel's island is the last of a long line of islands in books. Bordone's Isolario is a book of all the islands of the world with their maps, from the Venetian lagoon to the newly found Americas; Eco wrote about the isolarii in his essays on bibliophily. His copy is the 1534 edition.

source.label: Eco, La memoria vegetale e altri scritti di bibliofilia (2007), 'Sugli Isolari'

tours.title: Behind The Prague Cemetery
tours.blurb: Every character in the sixth novel except its forger existed, and every text he plagiarises is real: the serial novels of Sue and Dumas, the pamphlet that became the Protocols, the antisemitic and anti-Masonic literature of the nineteenth century. Eco owned most of it, and it fills the second cabinet.

stops.title: Il cimitero di Praga (2010)
stops.caption: Simone Simonini, forger and spy, assembles the document that will become the Protocols of the Elders of Zion out of the novels and pamphlets he has read. Eco's afterword says that apart from Simonini every character existed and did what the book says. Carlotta Eco recalls her father's extensive use of nineteenth-century engravings, mentioning The Prague Cemetery in particular.

source.label: Umberto Eco: La biblioteca del mondo (Davide Ferrario, 2022)

quote.text: Se dovessi raccontare la biblioteca di mio padre inizierei da qua: sono i feuilleton, i romanzi d'appendice dell'Ottocento che lui ha letto da ragazzo e che in parte ha letto anche a noi. E qui si trovano le immagini bellissime degli incisori del periodo, che lui poi ha utilizzato tantissimo soprattutto nei romanzi, Il cimitero di Praga.
quote.attribution: Carlotta Eco, in Davide Ferrario's film Umberto Eco: La biblioteca del mondo (2022)
quote.translation: If I had to tell the story of my father's library I would start from here: these are the feuilletons, the nineteenth-century serial novels that he read as a boy and that he partly read to us too. And here are the beautiful images by the engravers of the period, which he then used a great deal, especially in the novels, The Prague Cemetery.

stops.title: Maurice Joly, Dialogue aux enfers entre Machiavel et Montesquieu (1864)
stops.caption: Joly's satire of Napoleon III was extensively plagiarised in the antisemitic Protocols of the Elders of Zion. The identity of the compilers remains disputed; the traditional attribution to the Russian secret police is not securely established. Joly was jailed for the book. In the novel it is Rachkovsky of the tsar's secret police who takes delivery of Simonini's forgery, Eco's telling of the traditional account. Chapter 11 of the novel is called 'Joly'. The modern edition.

source.label: Eco, Six Walks in the Fictional Woods (1994), 'Fictional Protocols'; the novel, chapter 11

stops.title: Eugène Sue, Le Juif errant (1846)
stops.caption: Sue's Wandering Jew, the serial novel of 1844 with its world-spanning Jesuit conspiracy, was read by millions, and Simonini reads and reuses it. Eco traced the chain that runs from Sue and Dumas through Joly to the Protocols in one of his Harvard lectures, and had written on Sue's socialism long before. The illustrated Brussels edition of 1846.

source.label: Eco, Six Walks in the Fictional Woods (1994), 'Fictional Protocols'; Il superuomo di massa (1976), 'Eugène Sue: il socialismo e la consolazione'

stops.title: Eugène Sue, Oeuvres illustrées (1850)
stops.caption: The illustrated collected works of 1850, with two hundred drawings by Gavarni, Beaucé and Staal. Eco's two volumes hold Latréaumont, Mathilde and five other works; the Jesuit conspiracy that Simonini's memory is made of comes from Le Juif errant and Les Mystères du peuple, which are not among them. Carlotta Eco recalls her father's extensive use of nineteenth-century engravings, mentioning The Prague Cemetery in particular.

source.label: Umberto Eco: La biblioteca del mondo (Davide Ferrario, 2022); the Braidense record for the edition

quote.text: E qui si trovano le immagini bellissime degli incisori del periodo, che lui poi ha utilizzato tantissimo soprattutto nei romanzi, Il cimitero di Praga.
quote.translation: And here are the beautiful images by the engravers of the period, which he then used a great deal, especially in the novels, The Prague Cemetery.
quote.attribution: Carlotta Eco, in Davide Ferrario's film Umberto Eco: La biblioteca del mondo (2022)

stops.title: Compendio della vita di Giuseppe Balsamo, detto Cagliostro (1791)
stops.caption: The scene of the novel's title, a night meeting of rabbis among the graves of Prague, was copied by a German hack from Dumas's Joseph Balsamo, where Cagliostro assembles the conspirators of Europe. This is the Roman Inquisition's own life of the real Balsamo, printed in 1791, the year of his trial.

source.label: Eco, Six Walks in the Fictional Woods (1994), 'Fictional Protocols'

stops.title: Sir John Retcliffe (Hermann Goedsche), Biarritz
stops.caption: The German novel of 1868 whose chapter in the Jewish cemetery of Prague was soon circulated as a true report, the fiction turned into evidence. Chapter 14 of Eco's novel is titled 'Biarritz', after Goedsche's book, and Simonini watches his own invention being stolen. Eco's copy is a 1924 reprint.

source.label: Il cimitero di Praga, chapter 14

stops.title: Abbé Barruel, Mémoires pour servir à l'histoire du jacobinisme (1799)
stops.caption: The novel opens Simonini's education with his grandfather's letter to Barruel, the Jesuit who blamed the Revolution on Masons and Illuminati. The real letter, by a Captain Simonini of Florence, added the Jews to Barruel's plot, and that is where the modern conspiracy myth begins. The Augsburg edition of 1799.

source.label: Il cimitero di Praga, the grandfather's letter

stops.title: Gougenot des Mousseaux, La magie au dix-neuvième siècle (1864)
stops.caption: A Catholic gentleman who saw the devil in spiritualism and, five years after this book, published the Jew as the agent of Satan in history. Simonini feeds on him. Eco's copy is his earlier work on nineteenth-century magic.

source.label: Il cimitero di Praga

stops.title: Édouard Drumont, La France juive
stops.caption: First published in 1886, Drumont's two-volume antisemitic polemic became a major publishing success. Its author, later a deputy for Algiers, appears in the novel among the men Simonini serves. Eco's copy is the one-volume illustrated edition published by Blériot.

source.label: Il cimitero di Praga, the Paris chapters

stops.title: Alphonse Toussenel, Les juifs, rois de l'époque (1847)
stops.caption: The socialist version of the same hatred: a follower of Fourier who blamed the bankers, and the Jews as bankers, for the misery of the poor. He appears in the novel as a character, and Simonini builds his forgery on Toussenel's ideas. The second edition.

source.label: Il cimitero di Praga

stops.title: Léo Taxil, Les frères trois-points (1885)
stops.caption: Taxil, the ex-Freemason whose exposures of Masonic devil-worship fooled the Church for twelve years before he announced it had all been a hoax, is a main character of the novel. This is his book on the 'three-point brothers', the Masons, from the year of his convenient conversion.

source.label: Il cimitero di Praga, chapter 21

stops.title: La mistificazione di Leo Taxil (1897)
stops.caption: An Italian pamphlet printed the year Taxil stood up in Paris and confessed that the whole Palladian cult, its priestess and its demons had been his invention. The novel stages that confession.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Diana Vaughan, Mémoires d'une ex-palladiste
stops.caption: The converted priestess of Lucifer whose memoirs Taxil published in instalments, and who never existed. In the novel Simonini and Taxil manufacture her together, and Diana is the woman Simonini cannot remember. A modern reprint.

source.label: Il cimitero di Praga, the Taxil chapters

stops.title: J.-K. Huysmans, Là-bas (1891)
stops.caption: The black mass in the novel is taken from Huysmans's Là-bas, the decadent novel of Satanism in Paris that its author, a convert in the making, wrote from what he claimed was first-hand knowledge. Eco's copy is an 1891 printing, the fifth edition, from Tresse et Stock.

source.label: Il cimitero di Praga, the black mass

image.credit: Martin van Maele, illustration for Huysmans's La-bas, before 1926
image.alt: Martin van Maele's illustration of the black mass in Là-bas

stops.title: Freud, Studi sull'isteria
stops.caption: At the Café Magny Simonini meets a young Austrian doctor he calls Froïde, studying hysteria with Charcot, and starts a diary at his suggestion: the future inventor of the talking cure, treating the novel's narrator. The first volume of Freud's Italian collected works.

source.label: Il cimitero di Praga, chapter 3, 'Chez Magny'

stops.title: I Protocolli dei Savi anziani di Sion (1938)
stops.caption: Where the novel ends. First serialized in Russia in 1903, the forgery appeared in Sergei Nilus's book in 1905; The Times exposed it as a plagiarism of Joly in 1921, and it has been believed ever since. Eco's copy is a Fascist-era Italian edition. Fakes, he said, can produce real historical events; this one above all.

source.label: The Paris Review, 'Umberto Eco, The Art of Fiction No. 197' (2008)

quote.text: Another famous example is the Protocols of the Elders of Zion. It's a fake, but it corroborated Nazi ideology and in a sense paved the way to the Holocaust, because Hitler used the document to justify the destruction of Jews.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, interviewed by Lila Azam Zanganeh, The Paris Review, 'The Art of Fiction No. 197' (2008)

tours.title: Baudolino, Queen Loana and Numero zero
tours.blurb: Three novels and their sources: the chroniclers Baudolino lies to and the forged letter that sent explorers into Asia; the books of a Milan childhood that Queen Loana rebuilds a memory from; and the last novel, written in a year.

stops.title: Baudolino (2000)
stops.caption: A Piedmontese peasant boy adopted by Frederick Barbarossa becomes a liar whose lies come true: he forges the letter of Prester John, invents the Grail, and sets out to find the kingdom he made up. Eco's favourite theme, that a fake can make history, in the form of a picaresque.

source.label: The Paris Review, 'Umberto Eco, The Art of Fiction No. 197' (2008)

quote.text: Baudolino forges documents, devises utopias, constructs imaginary schemes about the future. His lies become real when his friends gaily embark on an actual journey to the legendary East.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, interviewed by Lila Azam Zanganeh, The Paris Review, 'The Art of Fiction No. 197' (2008)

stops.title: Otto of Freising, Chronica (Strasbourg, 1515)
stops.caption: The bishop who wrote the chronicle of the two cities and the deeds of Frederick, and who first mentioned Prester John, is Baudolino's teacher in the novel; the boy scrapes away the first version of Otto's chronicle to reuse the parchment, and the bishop's rewrite comes out kinder for it. Eco's copy is the first printed edition.

source.label: Baudolino, the Frederick chapters

stops.title: Niketas Choniates, Historia (1557)
stops.caption: The whole novel is told to Niketas Choniates, the Byzantine historian, during the sack of Constantinople in 1204 that his real history describes. Eco owned the first printed edition, Wolf's Greek and Latin text of 1557, and an Italian version of 1562.

source.label: Baudolino, the frame in Constantinople

stops.title: La lettera del Prete Gianni
stops.caption: The letter from the priest-king of the East that circulated from the 1160s, promising a Christian empire beyond the Muslims with rivers of jewels and a fountain of youth. It was a forgery, and it was believed for four centuries. In the novel Baudolino and his friends write it.

source.label: The Paris Review, 'Umberto Eco, The Art of Fiction No. 197' (2008)

quote.text: Just like the letter of Prester John: it was a forgery - and in my novel it was invented by none other than Baudolino himself - but it really incited medieval explorations of Asia because it described a fabulous Christian kingdom thriving somewhere in the mysterious Orient.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, interviewed by Lila Azam Zanganeh, The Paris Review, 'The Art of Fiction No. 197' (2008)

stops.title: Geo Pistarino, La nascita di Alessandria fra Genova e il Barbarossa (1968)
stops.caption: Alessandria, raised from the marshes in 1168 by the towns of the Lombard League as a fortress against Frederick Barbarossa, is Eco's own birthplace and the novel's: Baudolino watches the city rise and sees his father Gagliaudo's stratagem with the grain-fed cow end the emperor's siege of 1174 to 1175. Pistarino's study of the city's founding between Genoa and the emperor, printed in Alessandria, is dog-eared and underlined, with Eco's notes in the margin.

source.label: University of Bologna, the record of Eco's copy (ex-libris stamp, underlinings, dog-ears, marginal notes)

stops.title: La misteriosa fiamma della regina Loana (2004)
stops.caption: Yambo, a Milan antiquarian bookseller, wakes from a stroke with his reading intact and his life gone, and goes back to the family house to rebuild himself from the comics, songs and adventure novels of the 1930s and 40s. Eco called it an anti-Proust: a memory reconstructed from things instead of from within. A later Bompiani edition.

source.label: Umberto Eco, Sulla memoria, a conversation in three parts filmed by Davide Ferrario (2015), part 2

quote.text: Di lì quindi l'idea del libro che si può ricostruire la memoria privata attraverso brandelli di memoria pubblica: La misteriosa fiamma della regina Loana. In un certo senso il libro era l'anti-Proust, dove si ricostruiva la memoria su oggetti esterni e non su ricordi interni.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, Sulla memoria, filmed by Davide Ferrario (2015)
quote.translation: From there came the idea of a book in which private memory can be rebuilt out of scraps of public memory: The Mysterious Flame of Queen Loana. In a sense the book was the anti-Proust, where memory was reconstructed from external objects and not from inner recollections.

stops.title: Alexandre Dumas, Il conte di Montecristo
stops.caption: Yambo's grandfather's editions of Monte Cristo and the Musketeers are waiting in the attic, and they were waiting in Eco's own childhood too: his grandfather bound books, and a box of unbound novels by Gautier and Dumas in the cellar was the first library he ever raided. Eco defended Monte Cristo all his life as one of the most exciting novels ever written.

source.label: The Paris Review, 'Umberto Eco, The Art of Fiction No. 197' (2008)

quote.text: So he had a lot of unbound books lying here and there around his apartment - old, beautifully illustrated editions of popular nineteenth-century novels by Gautier and Dumas. Those were the first books I ever saw.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, interviewed by Lila Azam Zanganeh, The Paris Review, 'The Art of Fiction No. 197' (2008)

stops.title: Edmond Rostand, Cyrano de Bergerac (1898)
stops.caption: Cyrano runs through Queen Loana to its last pages: Yambo recites Rostand, and the finale returns to the school staircase where he waits for Lila to come down. Eco's copy is an early Paris edition of the play.

source.label: La misteriosa fiamma della regina Loana, the last chapters

stops.title: Ignatius Donnelly, The Great Cryptogram (1888)
stops.caption: Yambo's trade and Eco's hobby meet here: the literature that proves Bacon wrote Shakespeare. Donnelly, a Minnesota congressman who had already found Atlantis, filled a thousand pages with a cipher hidden in the First Folio that confesses it all. Eco collected the whole Baconian shelf; Theobald's Shakespeare Studies in Baconian Light stands a few books along from this one. A book about a secret nobody put there is the purest case of the reading he mistrusted.

source.label: Eco and Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2011), 'Every book published today is a post-incunabulum'

quote.text: My collection is very focused. It is a Bibliotheca Semiologica Curiosa Lunatica Magica et Pneumatica, or 'a collection dedicated to the occult and mistaken sciences'. For example, I have Ptolemy, who was wrong about the movement of the Earth, but not Galileo, who was right.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco in conversation with Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2009; English translation 2011), 'Every book published today is a post-incunabulum'

stops.title: Numero zero (2015)
stops.caption: The last novel: a Milan newspaper that will never appear, staffed to blackmail, and a journalist who believes Mussolini escaped in 1945 and a double was shot in his place. Eco said it took him only a year because part of it was his own memory and the rest was on the internet.

source.label: Louisiana Channel, 'Umberto Eco: I Was Always Narrating' (2015)

quote.text: For instance, why did this novel take me only one year? First, because part of the events were belonging to my personal memory. Second, because if you wanted the autopsy of Mussolini you find it immediately in the internet - you have not to make remote research.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, Louisiana Channel interview 'I Was Always Narrating' (2015)

tours.title: The Search for the Perfect Language
tours.blurb: Eco's 1993 history of Europe's attempts to recover the language of Adam or to build a better one was written out of this collection, and he said he rearranged the whole library around it. Chapter by chapter, the books he was reading: Dante and Lull, the kabbalists, the linguistic nationalists, the hieroglyphs, the ciphers, the magicians and the philosophical languages.

stops.title: La ricerca della lingua perfetta nella cultura europea (1993)
stops.caption: A history of a dream: from the Tower of Babel to Esperanto, Europe kept trying to find the one language God spoke to Adam, or to build a language so exact that error would be impossible. Eco wrote it out of the books in this room, and said the library was never the same afterwards.

source.label: Eco and Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2011), 'All the books we haven't read'

quote.text: While I was writing The Search for the Perfect Language I looked at my library anew, with new criteria, and changed it around. Which books would best nourish my thoughts on the subject? When I finished writing, some books went back on the linguistics shelf, and some to aesthetics, but others were already being used for a new piece of research.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco in conversation with Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2009; English translation 2011), 'All the books we haven't read'

stops.title: Dante, De vulgari eloquentia
stops.caption: Chapter 3. Dante's unfinished treatise on the vernacular is, for Eco, the first systematic project for a perfect language in Christian Europe: an illustrious Italian to be built out of the best of every dialect. Eco argued that Dante's idea of a form of speech given to Adam is startlingly close to what the kabbalist Abulafia was writing in the same years. The modern critical edition.

source.label: Eco, The Search for the Perfect Language (1993), chapter 3, 'The Perfect Language of Dante'

stops.title: Sefer Yetzirah, in Postel's Latin (1552)
stops.caption: Chapter 2. The Book of Formation, in which God makes the world by combining the twenty-two letters of the Hebrew alphabet, and the medieval kabbalists' permutations of the divine names: where Eco's history of the sacred reading of language begins. The first Latin translation, by Guillaume Postel.

source.label: Eco, The Search for the Perfect Language (1993), chapter 2, 'The Kabbalistic Pansemioticism'

stops.title: Ramon Lull, Opera (Strasbourg, 1598)
stops.caption: Chapter 4. The Majorcan mystic's Great Art: wheels of letters that combine the attributes of God into every possible proposition, invented in the 1270s to convert the infidel by demonstration. Eco reads it as the first combinatorial language and follows its fortune all the way to Leibniz and the computer. The Strasbourg collected edition.

source.label: Eco, The Search for the Perfect Language (1993), chapter 4, 'The Ars Magna of Raymond Lull'

stops.title: Ramon Lull, Arbor scientiae (1515)
stops.caption: Lull's tree of knowledge, in which every science grows from one trunk. Eco took the image up in From the Tree to the Labyrinth, whose title sets Lull's tree against the labyrinth of the modern encyclopaedia, where everything connects to everything and there is no trunk at all. The 1515 edition.

source.label: Eco, From the Tree to the Labyrinth (2007), chapter 1

image.credit: Ramon Llull; Library of Congress digitization
image.alt: The tree of knowledge from Lull's Arbor scientiae

stops.title: Guillaume Postel, La doctrine du siècle doré (1553)
stops.caption: Chapter 5. Postel, the Renaissance orientalist who held that Hebrew was the mother of all tongues, that the Gauls descended from Noah, and that a universal monarchy under the king of France would bring back the golden age. He ended in the care of a monastery, judged mad rather than heretical. One of his French tracts of 1553.

source.label: Eco and Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2011), 'Nothing can put an end to vanity'

quote.text: When I was working on my book about the search for the perfect language I came across some crazy linguists, inventors of wild theories about the roots of language. The most entertaining were the nationalists, who were totally convinced that their country's language was the language of Adam. According to Guillaume Postel, the Celts were descendants of Noah.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco in conversation with Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2009; English translation 2011), 'Nothing can put an end to vanity'

stops.title: Annius of Viterbo, Commentaria (1498)
stops.caption: Chapter 5 again. A Dominican who invented a lost Babylonian historian, Berosus, and published him to prove that Noah had settled Etruria and that Tuscan came before Latin. Eco calls this the first text of the nationalist theories of the mother tongue. The forgery was believed for a century. Eco's copy is the first edition, an incunabulum.

source.label: Eco, The Search for the Perfect Language (1993), chapter 5, 'The Monogenetic Hypothesis and the Mother Tongues'

stops.title: Goropius Becanus, Origines Antwerpianae (1569)
stops.caption: The Antwerp physician who proved that the language of Eden was Dutch, since the simplest words must be the oldest and Dutch had the shortest. Eco gave him his due in the chapter on the nationalist hypotheses, and to Carrière counted him among the 'crazy linguists' who each made their own nation's tongue the language of Adam. The first edition.

source.label: Eco and Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2011), 'Nothing can put an end to vanity'

quote.text: Goropius Becanus was convinced that every language stemmed from one primary language, the dialect of Antwerp. Abraham Mylius, on the other hand, showed how Hebrew had given rise to the Teutonic language, the purest form of the Antwerp dialect.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco in conversation with Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2009; English translation 2011), 'Nothing can put an end to vanity'

stops.title: Francesco Giorgi, De harmonia mundi (1525)
stops.caption: Chapter 6. A Venetian Franciscan's harmony of the world, in which Kabbalah, Pythagoras and Plato are tuned to the same musical scale; one of the Christian kabbalists Eco follows from Pico della Mirandola to Knorr von Rosenroth. Eco found this copy in New York and bought it for a fifth of the Milan price, because no American collector wanted a book in Latin.

source.label: Eco and Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2011), 'Every book published today is a post-incunabulum'

quote.text: I once found Francesco Giorgi's wonderful De Harmonia Mundi, published in 1525, at the highly reputed New York dealer Kraus, which sadly closed a few years ago. I had seen a copy in Milan, but thought it too expensive.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco in conversation with Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2009; English translation 2011), 'Every book published today is a post-incunabulum'

stops.title: Giordano Bruno, De umbris idearum (1582)
stops.caption: Chapter 6 ends with Bruno. The Shadows of Ideas, printed in Paris in 1582, turns Lull's wheels into a memory machine of images and an infinity of worlds; eighteen years later its author was burned in Rome. Eco's copy is the first edition.

source.label: Eco, The Search for the Perfect Language (1993), chapter 6, 'Bruno: Ars Combinatoria and Infinite Worlds'

image.alt: A memory diagram from Bruno's De umbris idearum (1582)

stops.title: Horapollo, Hieroglyphica (Basel, 1518)
stops.caption: Chapter 7. A late-antique book that told the Renaissance what the hieroglyphs meant: a vulture for a mother, a hare for openness, all of it wrong and all of it fertile for two centuries of emblems and allegories. Eco's copy is Froben's edition of 1518 of Bernardino Trebazio's Latin translation.

source.label: Eco, The Search for the Perfect Language (1993), chapter 7, 'The Perfect Language of Images'

stops.title: Pierio Valeriano, Hieroglyphica (1556)
stops.caption: The Renaissance encyclopaedia of hieroglyphs: fifty-eight books of sacred Egyptian letters, which Eco says reread the whole classical tradition in the light of Horapollo. The first edition, Basel 1556.

source.label: Eco, The Search for the Perfect Language (1993), chapter 7, 'The Perfect Language of Images'

image.alt: A page of Valeriano's Hieroglyphica (1556)

stops.title: Athanasius Kircher, Oedipus Aegyptiacus (1652 to 1654)
stops.caption: The centrepiece of chapter 7: Kircher's three folios deciphering the hieroglyphs as a hermetic wisdom, every reading wrong and the whole coherent. Eco told Carrière how he lectured on it at the Collège de France with the Sorbonne's Egyptologists in the front row, and how they loved it.

source.label: Eco and Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2011), 'Every book published today is a post-incunabulum'

quote.text: On the day of that class, the college porter said, 'Watch out, Professor sir. All the Sorbonne Egyptologists are in there, sitting in the front row.' I thought I was completely done for. … But I needn't have worried: the Egyptologists loved it. I realised they had never explored Kircher's work, having heard him described merely as a madman.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco in conversation with Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2009; English translation 2011), 'Every book published today is a post-incunabulum'

stops.title: Giulio Camillo, L'idea del theatro (in the Opere, 1566)
stops.caption: Chapter 7 also visits the memory theatre: a wooden amphitheatre, built for the king of France, in which all knowledge was to be arranged by images so that a man standing on the stage could take it in at a glance. Camillo died in 1544 with the theatre unfinished, and his description of it was published six years later, in 1550. Eco's copy is the collected works of 1566.

source.label: Eco, The Search for the Perfect Language (1993), chapter 7, 'The Perfect Language of Images'

stops.title: Johannes Romberch, Congestorium artificiosae memoriae (1520)
stops.caption: A Dominican's handbook of artificial memory, with alphabets made of objects and figures to be set in imaginary buildings. The memory palace is the oldest of Europe's information technologies, and Eco discusses these treatises beside Camillo. The Venice edition of 1520.

source.label: Eco, The Search for the Perfect Language (1993), chapter 7, 'The Perfect Language of Images'

stops.title: Trithemius, Polygraphiae libri sex (1550)
stops.caption: Chapters 6 and 9. The abbot's six books of polygraphy, printed in 1518, are the first printed treatise on ciphers: tables of words that hide a message inside what looks like a prayer. Eco follows Trithemius into the steganographies and then into Kircher's universal writing. The 1550 edition.

source.label: Eco, The Search for the Perfect Language (1993), chapter 9, 'Polygraphies'

stops.title: Giovanni Battista Della Porta, De furtivis literarum notis (1591)
stops.caption: The Neapolitan magus's book on secret writing, first printed in 1563, cited with Vigenère among the cipher books that carried Lull's combinatorics into cryptography. Della Porta also wrote on natural magic and on reading character from faces. The 1591 edition.

source.label: Eco, The Search for the Perfect Language (1993), chapter 6, 'Kabbalism and Lullism in the Steganographies'

stops.title: Blaise de Vigenère, Traicté des chiffres (1587)
stops.caption: Vigenère's treatise on ciphers of 1586, which gave its author's name to the polyalphabetic cipher that stood unbroken for three centuries, though he did not invent it. Eco cites it beside Della Porta. The 1587 printing.

source.label: Eco, The Search for the Perfect Language (1993), chapter 6, 'Kabbalism and Lullism in the Steganographies'

stops.title: Athanasius Kircher, Polygraphia nova (1663)
stops.caption: Chapter 9. Kircher's new and universal polygraphy: a dictionary by which the same numbered entries could be read in five languages, one of the first schemes for a writing that anyone could read whatever they spoke. The Rome edition of 1663.

source.label: Eco, The Search for the Perfect Language (1993), chapter 9, 'Kircher's Polygraphy'

stops.title: John Dee, Monas hieroglyphica (1564)
stops.caption: Chapter 8, the magic language. Dee's monad, a single glyph from which the alphabet and the cosmos unfold, and the angelic conversations he recorded; Eco reads the monad as a geometrical alphabet owing nothing to Hebrew. The first edition, Antwerp 1564.

source.label: Eco, The Search for the Perfect Language (1993), chapter 8, 'Dee's Magic Language'

stops.title: Fama Fraternitatis (1615)
stops.caption: The same chapter reads the Rosicrucian manifestos as a case of a secret language: a brotherhood that announces itself in print and promises a magical tongue, and a Europe that writes back to an address that does not exist. Eco's Fama is a 1615 printing bound with the Confessio.

source.label: Eco, The Search for the Perfect Language (1993), chapter 8, 'Magic Language'

stops.title: Comenius, Janua aurea reserata (1663)
stops.caption: Chapter 10. Comenius, the Moravian educator whose pansophia wanted a language in which things and words would match, is the bridge to the philosophical languages. This is his Golden Gate of Languages, the textbook that teaches Latin through the order of things, in a 1663 edition.

source.label: Eco, The Search for the Perfect Language (1993), chapter 10, 'A Priori Philosophical Languages'

stops.title: John Wilkins, An Essay towards a Real Character and a Philosophical Language (1668)
stops.caption: Chapter 12, a chapter to itself. The bishop who founded the Royal Society classified everything that exists into forty genera, with a character to write each thing and a word to say it: the most ambitious artificial language ever built, and the one Borges laughed at. Eco's copy is the first edition.

source.label: Eco, The Search for the Perfect Language (1993), chapter 12, 'John Wilkins'

stops.title: Leibniz, Collectanea etymologica (1717)
stops.caption: Chapter 14 goes from Leibniz to the Encyclopédie: the characteristica universalis, a calculus in which disputes would be settled by saying 'let us compute'. Eco's Leibniz is the posthumous collection of his writings on the origins and kinship of languages, printed in Hanover in 1717.

source.label: Eco, The Search for the Perfect Language (1993), chapter 14, 'From Leibniz to the Encyclopédie'

stops.title: Rivarol, De l'universalité de la langue française (1797)
stops.caption: Chapter 15. The Berlin Academy's prize essay of 1784, in which Rivarol asked why look for a universal language when French already was one, its word order being the order of reason itself. Eco enjoyed his verdicts on the competition.

source.label: Eco and Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2011), 'Nothing can put an end to vanity'

quote.text: Later there was Antoine de Rivarol, who claimed not that French was the original language, but that it was the most rational - English being too complicated, German too brutal, Italian too confused, etc.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco in conversation with Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2009; English translation 2011), 'Nothing can put an end to vanity'

tours.title: The essayist's masters
tours.blurb: Not the novels but fifty years of essays, and the books Eco wrote his thesis, his theory of signs, his readings and his lists out of: Aquinas, Pliny and Rabelais, Joyce, Nerval and Proust, Dumas and Fleming, Locke and Peirce, and the medieval aesthetics he began with.

stops.title: Il problema estetico in San Tommaso (1956)
stops.caption: Eco's first book, his doctoral thesis on the aesthetics of Thomas Aquinas, published when he was twenty-four. He kept his beloved Aquinas even after his faith went, and said that his father used to sit up late in the evening trying to make sense of a book he found thoroughly confusing. The Turin edition of 1956.

source.label: The Paris Review, 'Umberto Eco, The Art of Fiction No. 197' (2008)

quote.text: I started a thesis on the aesthetics of Thomas Aquinas, but right before I finished it my faith suffered a trauma. … But I continued to study the Middle Ages and medieval philosophy with great respect, not to mention my beloved Aquinas.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, interviewed by Lila Azam Zanganeh, The Paris Review, 'The Art of Fiction No. 197' (2008)

stops.title: Aquinas, Scriptum super primo Sententiarum (1498)
stops.caption: Aquinas's commentary on the first book of Peter Lombard's Sentences, the young theologian's first big work, in a 1498 incunabulum. Asked for his influences, Eco named Joyce and Borges to keep interviewers quiet, then added Aristotle, Aquinas and Locke.

source.label: The Paris Review, 'Umberto Eco, The Art of Fiction No. 197' (2008)

quote.text: Usually I say Joyce and Borges to keep the interviewer quiet, though it's not absolutely true. Just about everyone has influenced me. Joyce and Borges, certainly, but also Aristotle, Thomas Aquinas, John Locke - you name it.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, interviewed by Lila Azam Zanganeh, The Paris Review, 'The Art of Fiction No. 197' (2008)

stops.title: Edgar de Bruyne, L'esthétique du Moyen Âge
stops.caption: The Belgian historian whose three volumes opened medieval aesthetics beyond Aquinas. Eco's Art and Beauty in the Middle Ages credits him with the widening. The 1947 summary volume.

source.label: Eco, Art and Beauty in the Middle Ages (1959; revised 1987)

stops.title: Guillaume Durand, Rationale divinorum officiorum (1565)
stops.caption: A thirteenth-century explanation of the liturgy and of the meaning of every part of a church building, which Eco's Art and Beauty cites on the medieval way of reading images. Eco owned it twice: this 1565 edition and a 1480 incunabulum kept among his most precious books.

source.label: Eco, Art and Beauty in the Middle Ages (1959; revised 1987), notes to chapters 2 and 9

stops.title: Pliny, Naturalis historia (1487)
stops.caption: Thirty-seven books on everything in the world, from the stars to the uses of cabbage, written by a Roman admiral who died watching Vesuvius erupt. Eco called it the prototype of every encyclopaedia and opened his history of the tree of knowledge with it; The Infinity of Lists treats it as the great ancient list. A 1487 incunabulum.

source.label: Eco, The Infinity of Lists (2009); From the Tree to the Labyrinth (2007), section 1.3.1

stops.title: Vincent of Beauvais, Speculum doctrinale (1494)
stops.caption: The medieval encyclopaedia at its largest: Vincent's Great Mirror runs to eighty books and nearly ten thousand chapters, a Dominican's attempt to hold all knowledge in one work for Louis IX. This is the doctrinal mirror, one of its parts, in a 1494 incunabulum.

source.label: Eco, From the Tree to the Labyrinth (2007), section 1.3.2

stops.title: Rabelais, Oeuvres (Amsterdam, 1741)
stops.caption: The Infinity of Lists has a chapter called 'Excess, from Rabelais onwards', with Gargantua's two hundred games as the list that runs on for the sheer pleasure of running. Eco's Rabelais is the Amsterdam edition of 1741 with Le Duchat's notes.

source.label: Eco, The Infinity of Lists (2009), chapter 15

stops.title: James Joyce, Ulysses (Shakespeare and Company, 1924)
stops.caption: The last chapter of Eco's book on the open work grew into a book of its own on Joyce, from the Thomist order of the early work to the chaosmos of Finnegans Wake. Eco owned early Paris printings and noted, with a father's irony, that this was the one rare book his son admired.

source.label: Eco and Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2011), 'What will happen to your book collections when you die?'

quote.text: My children don't seem to. My son likes the fact that I own a first edition of Joyce's Ulysses, and my daughter often consults my Mattioli Herbarium from the sixteenth century, but that's about it. Having said that, I only became a true book lover around the age of fifty.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco in conversation with Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2009; English translation 2011), 'What will happen to your book collections when you die?'

stops.title: James Joyce, Finnegans Wake
stops.caption: The other pole of Le poetiche di Joyce, whose subtitle runs from the Summa to Finnegans Wake: the book of the night, written in a language of puns from sixty tongues, which Eco read as the model of the open work. A 1962 printing.

source.label: Eco, Le poetiche di Joyce (1966)

stops.title: Gérard de Nerval, Les filles du feu (1854)
stops.caption: Sylvie, the story Eco reread all his life, translated in 1999 and gave a whole Harvard lecture to, first appeared in the Revue des Deux Mondes in 1853 and was gathered into this collection of 1854, a year before its author hanged himself in a Paris alley. Eco's copy is the first edition.

source.label: Eco, Six Walks in the Fictional Woods (1994), 'The Woods of Loisy'; On Literature (2002), 'The Mists of the Valois'

stops.title: Nerval, Sylvie, translated by Umberto Eco (1999)
stops.caption: Eco's own translation of the story, for Einaudi's series of writers translated by writers. His book on translation, Dire quasi la stessa cosa, grew partly out of the problems it set him. It was the first book he gave his grandson, who admits he has not yet read it.

source.label: Umberto Eco: La biblioteca del mondo (Davide Ferrario, 2022)

quote.text: Il primo libro che mi ha regalato è stato Sylvie di Nerval, e posso già anticipare che non l'ho ancora letto.
quote.attribution: Emanuele Eco, his grandson, in Davide Ferrario's film Umberto Eco: La biblioteca del mondo (2022)
quote.translation: The first book he gave me was Nerval's Sylvie, and I can tell you now that I have not read it yet.

stops.title: Proust, À la recherche du temps perdu
stops.caption: Proust's pages on Nerval are the guide Eco follows into Sylvie, and Queen Loana was conceived as an anti-Proust, a memory rebuilt from objects rather than from within. One volume of the Recherche, the second, in Italian.

source.label: Eco, Six Walks in the Fictional Woods (1994), 'The Woods of Loisy'

stops.title: Mémoires de M. d'Artagnan (Cologne, 1700)
stops.caption: The apocryphal memoirs by Courtilz de Sandras from which Dumas took his Musketeers. Eco spent a whole lecture on The Three Musketeers and the house in the rue Servandoni where Aramis lives in 1625, a street named after an architect who was born in 1695. Eco's copy is the Cologne edition of 1700.

source.label: Eco, Six Walks in the Fictional Woods (1994), 'The Strange Case of the Rue Servandoni'

stops.title: Ian Fleming, Casino Royale
stops.caption: Eco's structural analysis of the Bond plot appeared in 1965, one of the first serious readings of a spy novel; he was still boasting of it over a calzone forty years later. Six Walks reads the death of Le Chiffre in this book as a lesson in how a text sets its pace. The Italian edition.

source.label: The Paris Review, 'Umberto Eco, The Art of Fiction No. 197' (2008)

quote.text: Did you know that I once published a structural analysis of the archetypal Ian Fleming plot?
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, as reported by Lila Azam Zanganeh in her introduction to The Paris Review's 'The Art of Fiction No. 197' (2008)

stops.title: Italo Calvino, Lezioni americane
stops.caption: Six Walks opens with Calvino, who died in 1985 before he could give his own Norton lectures at Harvard. His Six Memos for the Next Millennium are the book Eco's six lectures set out from, eight years later by Eco's own count in the first of them.

source.label: Eco, Six Walks in the Fictional Woods (1994), 'Entering the Woods'

stops.title: John Locke, An Essay concerning Humane Understanding (1690)
stops.caption: The book that named the science of signs. In its last chapter Locke divides all knowledge into physics, ethics and semiotics, and Eco repeated in several places that his discipline was founded there in 1690. His copy is the first edition; Eco also owned an 1823 printing in three volumes.

source.label: Eco, The Search for the Perfect Language (1993), introduction; Semiotics and the Philosophy of Language (1984)

stops.title: Charles Sanders Peirce, Collected Papers
stops.caption: The other founder of Eco's semiotics: Peirce's interpretant and his unlimited semiosis, each sign explained by another sign without end, carry A Theory of Semiotics, and Kant and the Platypus returns to him on perception. The first volume of the Collected Papers.

source.label: Eco, A Theory of Semiotics (1976); Kant and the Platypus (1997)

stops.title: Joseph de Maistre, Les soirées de Saint-Pétersbourg (1821)
stops.caption: Eco's Serendipities closes with the linguistics of Joseph de Maistre: the reactionary's theory, set out in these dialogues, that etymology reveals a lost divine wisdom, so that every word proves the Fall. The first edition of 1821.

source.label: Eco, Serendipities (1998), 'The Linguistics of Joseph de Maistre'

stops.title: Cosmas Indicopleustes, Topographie chrétienne
stops.caption: A sixth-century monk who drew the earth flat, shaped like the tabernacle of Moses. Eco showed that the medieval West never read him, and that the belief that the Middle Ages thought the earth flat was invented in the nineteenth century: a false idea about false ideas. The third volume of the French edition.

source.label: Eco, Serendipities (1998), 'The Force of Falsity'

tours.title: Eco's own books
tours.blurb: Eco's own books, from the thesis to the last novel, some in copies from his own shelves, the others in the copies the Braidense keeps in its reference section, with what he said about each: the thesis, the open work, the comics and Superman, the theory of signs, the novels, the lists, and the translations that fill a bookcase in the study.

stops.title: Il nome della rosa (1980)
stops.caption: More than ten million copies later, Eco affected to hate the book. He told audiences he hoped they hated it too, since the five novels he had written since were better. It began with a list of monks' names and a letter to a chemist about how to poison a reader.

source.label: Umberto Eco: La biblioteca del mondo (Davide Ferrario, 2022)

quote.text: Sono tornato a casa e ho cominciato a buttar giù una lista di nomi di monaci, e poi ho scritto a un amico chimico come si può avvelenare una persona mentre legge un libro. Lui mi ha risposto, poi ho distrutto la lettera.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, in Davide Ferrario's film Umberto Eco: La biblioteca del mondo (2022)
quote.translation: I went home and started jotting down a list of monks' names, and then I wrote to a chemist friend asking how one can poison a person while he is reading a book. He answered me, then I destroyed the letter.

stops.title: Il pendolo di Foucault (1988)
stops.caption: The novel of the conspiracy that becomes true because people believe it. Eco confirmed that Belbo playing the trumpet in the cemetery is his own memory, and confessed that in his seventies he had bought himself a trumpet to get his childhood back.

source.label: The Paris Review, 'Umberto Eco, The Art of Fiction No. 197' (2008)

quote.text: That scene is absolutely autobiographical. I am not Belbo, but it happened to me and it was so important that now I will reveal something that I've never said before. Three months ago I bought a high-quality trumpet for about two thousand dollars.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, interviewed by Lila Azam Zanganeh, The Paris Review, 'The Art of Fiction No. 197' (2008)

stops.title: Opera aperta (1976 printing)
stops.caption: The 1962 essay on the open work, on Joyce, Mallarmé and the music of Berio and Stockhausen, made Eco's name. It came out three months before his father died, and got a review from the poet Montale that Eco treasured for his father's sake.

source.label: The Paris Review, 'Umberto Eco, The Art of Fiction No. 197' (2008)

quote.text: The Open Work was published exactly three months before his death and was reviewed by the great poet Eugenio Montale in the Corriere della Sera. It was a mixed review - curious, friendly, and nasty - but it was a review by Montale nonetheless and I think that, for my father, it would have been impossible to imagine anything more.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, interviewed by Lila Azam Zanganeh, The Paris Review, 'The Art of Fiction No. 197' (2008)

stops.title: Apocalittici e integrati (1964)
stops.caption: The book with which Eco turned to television, comics and the detective novel, and told Italian intellectuals that Superman and Charlie Brown deserved the same attention as Joyce. Its title gave Italian the two words for the culture pessimist and the happy consumer. The Bompiani edition of 1964.

source.label: Umberto Eco: La biblioteca del mondo (Davide Ferrario, 2022)

quote.text: A un certo punto, col libro Apocalittici e integrati, passo a occuparmi di quelle che sono dette le comunicazioni di massa: la televisione, i fumetti, il romanzo giallo.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, in Davide Ferrario's film Umberto Eco: La biblioteca del mondo (2022)
quote.translation: At a certain point, with the book Apocalittici e integrati, I turned to what are called mass communications: television, comics, the detective novel.

stops.title: Trattato di semiotica generale (1975)
stops.caption: Eco's theory of signs, the book that made him a professor of semiotics at Bologna. Its most quoted line defines a sign as anything that can be used to lie, and he traced his lifelong interest in fakes back to it.

source.label: Umberto Eco: La biblioteca del mondo (Davide Ferrario, 2022)

quote.text: Ho cominciato negli anni Settanta a occuparmi della bugia. Nel mio Trattato di semiotica generale si dice che il segno è tutto ciò che può essere usato per mentire, una definizione che ha avuto qualche fortuna. Di lì l'interesse per il falso.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, in Davide Ferrario's film Umberto Eco: La biblioteca del mondo (2022)
quote.translation: I began in the 1970s to concern myself with the lie. In my Theory of Semiotics it is said that a sign is everything that can be used to lie, a definition that has enjoyed some success. From there came the interest in the fake.

stops.title: Lector in fabula (1979)
stops.caption: The reader in the story: here Eco drew his distinction between the empirical reader, who exists, and the model reader, whom a serious author constructs and then teaches how to read the book.

source.label: Louisiana Channel, 'Umberto Eco: I Was Always Narrating' (2015)

quote.text: I wrote a book called 'Lector in Fabula' about narrativity in which I make a radical distinction between the empirical reader and the model reader. The empirical reader is the reader which exists.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, Louisiana Channel interview 'I Was Always Narrating' (2015)

stops.title: Come si fa una tesi di laurea (1977)
