stops.caption: How to write a thesis: the little manual that has guided Italian students since 1977 and has been translated into many languages. Its first rule was never to choose a contemporary subject; most theses now do, Eco told Carrière, and piles of them are about his own work.

source.label: Eco and Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2011), 'It took chickens almost a century to learn not to cross the road'

quote.text: In the Seventies I wrote a book called How to Write a Thesis, which has been translated into lots of languages. The first of my many tips was never to choose a contemporary subject. … And yet most of today's theses explore contemporary issues. I receive loads of theses about my own work. It's crazy. How can you write a thesis about a guy who is still alive?
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco in conversation with Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2009; English translation 2011), 'It took chickens almost a century to learn not to cross the road'

stops.title: Il superuomo di massa (1976)
stops.caption: The essays on the popular novel: the tears of Salgari's Black Corsair, Sue's socialism and consolation, the Beati Paoli, and the rise of the superman of the masses from Monte Cristo to Tarzan. Eco read the feuilleton with the same seriousness as Joyce, and the same pleasure.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of the 1976 edition

stops.title: Il caso Bond (1965)
stops.caption: The volume Eco edited with Oreste Del Buono on James Bond, with his own structural reading of the Fleming plot: the same moves in the same order in every novel, like a game of chess. He was still proud of it forty years later.

source.label: The Paris Review, 'Umberto Eco, The Art of Fiction No. 197' (2008)

stops.title: I fumetti di Mao (1971)
stops.caption: Chinese comics of the Cultural Revolution, collected by a journalist in China and published in Italy with Eco among the editors. Eco remembered them as oddly pacifist, giving no hint of what was happening in the country that made them.

source.label: Eco and Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2011), 'Fire as censor'

quote.text: In 1971 I contributed to a book about Chinese comics. A journalist based in China had collected together all kinds of material: comic books in the English style, but also photo stories. The comics had been created during the Cultural Revolution, but they gave no indication whatsoever of what was happening in China at the time.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco in conversation with Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2009; English translation 2011), 'Fire as censor'

stops.title: I limiti dell'interpretazione (1990)
stops.caption: Where Eco built his theory of fakes and forgeries, and answered the readers who found too much in his novels: a text has limits, and not every reading is as good as every other. He explained why his narrator is called Casaubon in his Cambridge lectures of 1990, published as Interpretation and Overinterpretation.

source.label: Eco and Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2011), 'Every book published today is a post-incunabulum'

quote.text: I am fascinated by error, by bad faith and idiocy. Like Flaubert. You and I both adore silliness. … In The Limits of Interpretation I create a theory of fakes and forgeries.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco in conversation with Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2009; English translation 2011), 'Every book published today is a post-incunabulum'

stops.title: Kant e l'ornitorinco (1997)
stops.caption: Essays on cognition and language, on how a platypus fits the categories when it turns up with a duck's bill and a beaver's tail: the return to Peirce and Kant after the semiotics of the 1970s. The Bompiani edition of 1997.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of the edition

stops.title: Vertigine della lista (2009)
stops.caption: The book of lists, written for the Louvre: from Homer's catalogue of ships to the litanies of the saints, from Rabelais to the telephone directory, why culture keeps making lists of things it cannot grasp whole. Eco said the list was the origin of culture.

source.label: Der Spiegel, 'We Like Lists Because We Don't Want to Die' (2009)

quote.text: The list is the origin of culture. It's part of the history of art and literature. What does culture want? To make infinity comprehensible. It also wants to create order - not always, but often. And how, as a human being, does one face infinity? How does one attempt to grasp the incomprehensible? Through lists, through catalogs, through collections in museums and through encyclopedias and dictionaries.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, interviewed by Der Spiegel, 'We Like Lists Because We Don't Want to Die' (2009)

stops.title: La memoria vegetale e altri scritti di bibliofilia (2007)
stops.caption: Eco's essays on book collecting, named for the memory kept in paper, which is made of plants: on catalogues, on the joy of the hunt, on the isolarii and on how to justify a private library to the visitor who asks whether you have read them all.

source.label: Eco and Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2011), 'All the books we haven't read'

quote.text: There are several ways of responding to the person who comes to your house, notices your impressive library and can only think to ask, 'Have you read them all?' … Personally, I've two replies. The first: 'No. These are just the books I'm planning to read next week. The ones I've already read are at the university.'
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco in conversation with Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2009; English translation 2011), 'All the books we haven't read'

stops.title: Bookcase Q: Eco in translation
stops.caption: Across the flat, in the big study, a whole bookcase of Eco's own books in translation, dozens of languages with Arabic and Japanese among them, and the books written about him.

source.label: Umberto Eco: A Library of the World, the subtitled clip (2022)

quote.text: They are my books, translations... and they are books on me.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, in Davide Ferrario's film Umberto Eco: La biblioteca del mondo (2022)

tours.title: The strangest books in the rare room
tours.blurb: Eco called his rare-book collection a Bibliotheca semiologica curiosa lunatica magica et pneumatica: a library of occult and mistaken sciences. This tour picks the most extraordinary volumes in it, from the most beautiful book of the fifteenth century to a Jesuit's map of the fires under the earth.

stops.title: Hypnerotomachia Poliphili (Venice, Aldus Manutius, 1499)
stops.caption: Poliphilo's dream of love, printed by Aldus in 1499 with its famous woodcuts, is the book collectors call the most beautiful of the fifteenth century. Eco's copy is the first edition. He liked to point out that his neighbour in Milan owned one too, and that the Castello Sforzesco across the square held a third.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

quote.text: Incidentally, it turns out that this neighbour and I both own a copy of the Hypnerotomachia Poliphili, or Poliphilo's Strife of Love in a Dream — possibly the most beautiful book in the world. We laugh because, right across from our building, the famous Castello Sforzesco library contains a third copy of this same Hypnerotomachia, so our little spot has without question the highest concentration of Hypnerotomachiae anywhere in the world!
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco in conversation with Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2009; English translation 2011)

image.credit: Aldus Manutius / Francesco Colonna, 1499; scan via Herzog August Bibliothek Wolfenbuttel
image.alt: Woodcut of an elephant carrying an obelisk, from the Hypnerotomachia Poliphili (1499)

stops.title: Hartmann Schedel, the Nuremberg Chronicle (1493)
stops.caption: A history of the world from Creation to the 1490s with more than 1,800 woodcuts, the most heavily illustrated book of its century. Eco named it among the incunabula a collector cannot do without, and enjoyed the fact that its printers reused the same city view for several different cities.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

quote.text: The Nuremberg Chronicle — an illustrated history of the world from Creation to the 1490s — sometimes uses the same plate to represent different cities. It shows us how printers often prioritised illustration over information.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco in conversation with Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2009; English translation 2011)

image.credit: Michael Wolgemut workshop (woodcut), Hartmann Schedel text, 1493
image.alt: The double-page view of Nuremberg from the Nuremberg Chronicle (1493)

stops.title: Ptolemy, Almagest (1528)
stops.caption: The rule of the whole collection, stated in one sentence: Eco kept the astronomer who put the earth at the centre of the universe and left out the one who moved it. He also told the story of a Ptolemy incunabulum he passed over at 100,000 euros; three weeks later a similar copy sold at auction for 700,000.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

quote.text: So I collect books about subjects in which I don't believe, like kabbalah, alchemy, magic, invented languages. Books that lie, albeit unwittingly. I have Ptolemy, not Galileo, because Galileo told the truth. I prefer lunatic science.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, interviewed by Lila Azam Zanganeh, The Paris Review, 'The Art of Fiction No. 197' (2008)

stops.title: Athanasius Kircher, Oedipus Aegyptiacus (Rome, 1652 to 1654)
stops.caption: Three volumes in which the Jesuit polymath announced that he had deciphered the hieroglyphs. He had not: his readings were mystical inventions, and Champollion later showed that a cartouche Kircher read as a hymn spelled the name of a pharaoh. Kircher was Eco's great collecting passion; he owned every book the man printed but one.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

quote.text: I have all his books except the Ars Magnesia, which is impossible to get hold of, despite being a small book with no illustrations. Kircher wasn't yet known at the time of publication, so I expect only a few copies were printed. Also, the book is so devoid of charm that probably no one thought it worth saving.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco in conversation with Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2009; English translation 2011)

image.alt: Frontispiece of Kircher's Oedipus Aegyptiacus (1652)

stops.title: Athanasius Kircher, Mundus subterraneus (Amsterdam, 1664 to 1665)
stops.caption: Kircher's tour of the interior of the earth: a web of fire channels feeding the volcanoes, underground oceans, the origin of springs, dragons in caves, and a map placing Atlantis in the middle of the ocean. He had climbed into the crater of Vesuvius to look for himself.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

image.alt: Kircher's diagram of the fires inside the earth, from Mundus subterraneus (1665)

stops.title: Athanasius Kircher, China illustrata (Amsterdam, 1667)
stops.caption: Kircher never went to China; he compiled the reports of his fellow Jesuits into the first European encyclopaedia of the country, complete with a comparison of Chinese characters and Egyptian hieroglyphs. Eco used that comparison in his history of the search for a perfect language.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

quote.text: A Chinese character was monogamously bound to the concept it represented; that was its limitation: an Egyptian hieroglyph showed its superiority by its ability to summon up entire 'texts,' and to express complex chunks of infinitely interpretable content.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, The Search for the Perfect Language (1993; English translation by James Fentress, 1995), on Kircher's reading of Chinese

image.alt: Frontispiece of Kircher's China illustrata (1667)

stops.title: Athanasius Kircher, Ars magna lucis et umbrae (Rome, 1646)
stops.caption: The great art of light and shadow: sundials and moondials, mirrors, the colours of the rainbow, the anatomy of the eye, and the projection of painted images onto a wall, which made Kircher one of the ancestors of the magic lantern.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

image.alt: Frontispiece of Kircher's Ars magna lucis et umbrae (1646)

stops.title: Athanasius Kircher, Musurgia universalis (Rome, 1650)
stops.caption: Everything about sound, from birdsong written out in notes to the echo, the speaking tube and the hearing of the deaf. It also describes a box of wooden rods with which anyone, musical or not, could compose a four-part hymn: a composing machine centuries before the computer.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

image.alt: Frontispiece of Kircher's Musurgia universalis (1650)

stops.title: Athanasius Kircher, Turris Babel (Amsterdam, 1679)
stops.caption: Kircher's last book, on the Tower of Babel and the confusion of tongues. He calculated that a tower reaching the moon would have needed more material than the earth contains and would have tipped the globe off its centre. The confusion of languages that followed Babel is the starting point of Eco's own history of the perfect language.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

image.alt: The Tower of Babel, a plate from Kircher's Turris Babel (1679)

stops.title: Robert Fludd, Utriusque cosmi historia (Oppenheim, 1617 to 1621)
stops.caption: Fludd's history of the two worlds, the great cosmos and the small one that is man, opens with a black square: the nothing before Creation, labelled 'and so on to infinity' on all four sides. Eco's friend Jean-Claude Carrière owned a set too, and told him how it had reached him.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

quote.text: The Fludd came to me via a broker who used to go round on a moped, carting these treasures with him in a plastic bag on his handlebars. It took me four years to pay for the set.
quote.attribution: Jean-Claude Carrière, on his own set of Fludd, in conversation with Umberto Eco, This Is Not the End of the Book (2009; English translation 2011), 'Every book published today is a post-incunabulum'

image.credit: Robert Fludd, 1617 (Tractatus I, Liber I, p.26)
image.alt: Robert Fludd's black square, the void before Creation, captioned Et sic in infinitum (1617)

stops.title: Michael Maier, Atalanta fugiens (Oppenheim, 1617 to 1618)
stops.caption: An alchemical emblem book that is also a piece of music: fifty engravings by Matthäus Merian, each with an epigram and a three-voice fugue to be sung. Emblem 21 sets the alchemist the geometer's task of drawing a circle around a triangle around a square around a man and a woman.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

image.credit: Michael Maier, engraved by Matthaeus Merian, 1617
image.alt: Emblem 21 of Maier's Atalanta fugiens: the geometer with the circle, triangle and square (1617)

stops.title: Heinrich Khunrath, Amphitheatrum sapientiae aeternae (Hanau, 1609)
stops.caption: The amphitheatre of eternal wisdom, a Christian alchemist's summa whose plates show the adept kneeling in an oratory that opens onto a laboratory, prayer and furnace under one roof. It is one of the sources of the Rosicrucian imagery that fills Foucault's Pendulum.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

image.credit: Hans Vredeman de Vries, for Khunrath's Amphitheatrum sapientiae aeternae (1595)
image.alt: The alchemist's oratory and laboratory, designed by Hans Vredeman de Vries for Khunrath's Amphitheatrum sapientiae aeternae

stops.title: John Dee, Monas hieroglyphica (Antwerp, 1564)
stops.caption: Queen Elizabeth's astrologer compressed the sun, the moon, the four elements and the sign of Aries into a single glyph and claimed it held the secret of the whole of creation. He wrote the book in twelve days.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

image.alt: Title page of John Dee's Monas hieroglyphica (1564) with the monad sign

stops.title: Aegidius Gutman, Offenbarung göttlicher Majestät (1619)
stops.caption: A German mystic's revelation of divine majesty, considered the inspiration behind the Rosicrucian manifestos. Eco spotted it filed under Theology in a Munich auction catalogue and had it bought for 150 euros; every page carries manuscript notes in red, black and green Gothic script.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

quote.text: I did a bit of research and found out that Gutman is considered the inspiration behind all the Rosicrucian manifestos, but that his book had never appeared in a catalogue on the subject, at least not for the last thirty years. It was being auctioned for an initial asking price of 100 euros in today's money. I hoped it might escape the attention of collectors as it should really have been in the 'Occult' section.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco in conversation with Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2009; English translation 2011)

stops.title: Malleus maleficarum (1492)
stops.caption: The hammer of witches, the manual that taught inquisitors how to identify, try and burn them. Eco's copy is an incunabulum with a story attached to its binding.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

quote.text: I own an incunabulum of the influential and deadly witch-hunting manual, the Malleus Maleficarum. It was bound by a certain 'Horned Moses', which is to say a Jew, who worked for the Cistercian libraries only, and who did in fact sign each binding (in itself rather a rare practice by the end of the fifteenth century) with an image of a Moses with horns. What a story that is!
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco in conversation with Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2009; English translation 2011)

image.alt: Title page of a 1520 Malleus maleficarum

stops.title: Frederik Ruysch, Thesaurus anatomicus (Amsterdam, 1701 to 1716; this printing 1739)
stops.caption: The Amsterdam anatomist's catalogue of his cabinet of preserved specimens, with plates of small skeletons arranged in weeping tableaux among trees of dried arteries. Eco's grandson remembers being shown the plates in place of the cartoons he was not allowed to watch.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

image.credit: Cornelis Huyberts (engraver) after Frederik Ruysch, 1701-1716; Wellcome Collection (CC BY 4.0)
image.alt: A tableau of small skeletons from Ruysch's Thesaurus anatomicus

stops.title: Michael Scot, Liber phisionomiae (Venice, 1477)
stops.caption: The court astrologer of the emperor Frederick II explains how to read character in a face. Dante put Michael Scot among the sorcerers in Hell. Physiognomy is one of the headings of Eco's arrangement of his collection, beside magic, alchemy and the rest of the mistaken sciences.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Ulisse Aldrovandi, Serpentum et draconum historiae (Bologna, 1640)
stops.caption: The Bologna naturalist's history of snakes and dragons, one of the volumes of the natural history he left unfinished at his death. Eco's family recall that these were the plates he brought out for the grandchildren.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

quote.text: Ai nipoti mostrava con divertimento gli animali, i mostri e le creature dai libri di Aldrovandi e Kircher, agli altri anche l'Atalanta fugiens colorata di Meyer [Maier], o la splendida composizione delle pagine della Hypnerotomachia Poliphili, stampata da Aldo Manuzio nel 1499.
quote.attribution: Renate Ramge, Carlotta Eco and Stefano Eco, statement for the opening of the Eco room at the Braidense (ANSA, 4 May 2022)
quote.translation: To his grandchildren he showed with amusement the animals, monsters and creatures from the books of Aldrovandi and Kircher; to others also Maier's coloured Atalanta fugiens, or the splendid page composition of the Hypnerotomachia Poliphili, printed by Aldus Manutius in 1499.

image.credit: Ulisse Aldrovandi, Monstrorum historia (1642); photograph by Sailko, CC BY 3.0
image.alt: A headless man from Aldrovandi's Monstrorum historia (1642)

stops.title: Bernhard von Breydenbach, Le grant voyage de Jhérusalem (Paris, 1517)
stops.caption: The French version of the first illustrated travel book, a pilgrimage to the Holy Land drawn on the spot by the artist Erhard Reuwich, with fold-out views of Venice and Jerusalem. Asked which book he would carry out of a fire, Eco chose his Latin Breydenbach.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

quote.text: Perhaps I would take Bernhard von Breydenbach's Peregrinatio in Terram Sanctam, Spier, Drach, 1490, on account of its wonderful illustrated plates on several folded pages.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco in conversation with Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2009; English translation 2011)

stops.title: Pietro Andrea Mattioli, Commentarii in sex libros Pedacii Dioscoridis (Venice, 1565)
stops.caption: The great illustrated herbal of the sixteenth century, Mattioli's commentary on Dioscorides with hundreds of woodcuts of plants. Of all the rare books, Eco said, this was the one his daughter actually consulted.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

quote.text: My son likes the fact that I own a first edition of Joyce's Ulysses, and my daughter often consults my Mattioli Herbarium from the sixteenth century, but that's about it. Having said that, I only became a true book lover around the age of fifty.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco in conversation with Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2009; English translation 2011)

stops.title: Le chef-d'oeuvre d'un inconnu (1714; this edition 1716)
stops.caption: A hoax by Thémiseul de Saint-Hyacinthe: a trivial little song buried under a mountain of learned commentary by an imaginary doctor, a parody of scholarly editing that Eco singled out as particularly dear to him.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

quote.text: Da questo punto di vista mi è particolarmente caro un libro, Le chef-d'oeuvre d'un inconnu … Il libro è del 1714 e dietro l'immaginario dottor Matanasius si cela in realtà Thémiseul de Saint-Hyacinthe. Non gode di particolare attenzione nella storia della letteratura, nemmeno da parte degli esperti di opere eccentriche, ed è un peccato.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, in Davide Ferrario's film Umberto Eco: La biblioteca del mondo (2022)
quote.translation: From this point of view one book is particularly dear to me, Le chef-d'oeuvre d'un inconnu. The book is from 1714, and behind the imaginary Doctor Matanasius hides Thémiseul de Saint-Hyacinthe. It gets no particular attention in the history of literature, not even from the experts on eccentric works, and that is a pity.

stops.title: Raimondo di Sangro, Lettera apologetica (Naples, 1750)
stops.caption: The Prince of Sansevero, alchemist and Freemason, wrote this letter to defend the knotted cords of the Incas as a true writing system, complete with coloured plates of quipus. Eco loved the chain that led to it: a French novel about a Peruvian woman, read by a Neapolitan prince.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

quote.text: The Neapolitan prince and alchemist Raimondo di Sangro studied Mme de Graffigny's book in great depth and produced that wonderful illustrated book about quipus. This Prince of Sansevero was a remarkable character. He was an occultist and most likely a Freemason as well, and is best known for decorating his chapel in Naples with sculptures of skinless human bodies with visible venous systems.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco in conversation with Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2009; English translation 2011)

stops.title: Biblia sacra vulgatae editionis (1758 edition)
stops.caption: The Clementine Vulgate, the Latin Bible as fixed by the Counter-Reformation popes in 1592, in an eighteenth-century printing. A collection of lunatic science needs the book everything else argued with, and this is the one Eco kept in the rare room.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

tours.title: Books that lie
tours.blurb: Eco began as a theorist of the sign, which he defined as anything that can be used to lie, and from there went on to collect forgeries, hoaxes and the works of the literary madmen. This tour follows the false through the shelves, from a forged Babylonian history to the Protocols.

stops.title: Umberto Eco, Trattato di semiotica generale (1975)
stops.caption: The theory of semiotics that made Eco's academic name contains the definition from which his whole library of the false grew: a sign is anything that can be used to lie.

source.label: Umberto Eco, A Theory of Semiotics (1975)

quote.text: Ho cominciato negli anni Settanta a occuparmi della bugia. Nel mio Trattato di semiotica generale si dice che il segno è tutto ciò che può essere usato per mentire, una definizione che ha avuto qualche fortuna. Di lì l'interesse per il falso.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, in Davide Ferrario's film Umberto Eco: La biblioteca del mondo (2022)
quote.translation: In the 1970s I began to concern myself with the lie. My Theory of Semiotics says that a sign is everything that can be used to lie, a definition that has enjoyed some success. From there came the interest in the fake.

stops.title: Annius of Viterbo, Commentaria super opera diversorum auctorum de antiquitatibus (Rome, 1498)
stops.caption: The most successful forgery of the Renaissance. Annius, a Dominican, published 'lost' works of the Babylonian priest Berosus and other ancient authors, all written by himself, which gave every nation in Europe a founder descended from Noah. Historians quoted him for a century.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Berosus Babilonicus, De his quae praecesserunt inundationem terrarum (1510)
stops.caption: Annius's forged Berosus travelling on its own, reprinted in a handy edition as if it were a real chronicle of the world before the Flood. Eco followed these inventions in his history of the search for the original language, where Annius supplies half of Europe's imaginary ancestors.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: The Letter of Prester John
stops.caption: A twelfth-century letter from a Christian emperor of the Indies, describing a kingdom of marvels, that circulated in hundreds of copies and sent travellers east for three hundred years. Nobody wrote it. In Baudolino, Eco gives the job to his hero.

source.label: Umberto Eco, Baudolino (2000)

quote.text: Just like the letter of Prester John: it was a forgery—and in my novel it was invented by none other than Baudolino himself—but it really incited medieval explorations of Asia because it described a fabulous Christian kingdom thriving somewhere in the mysterious Orient.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, interviewed by Lila Azam Zanganeh, The Paris Review, 'The Art of Fiction No. 197' (2008)

stops.title: Giuseppe Vella, Libro del Consiglio di Egitto (Palermo, 1793)
stops.caption: A Maltese chaplain in Palermo invented an Arabic chronicle of Sicily's Norman kings out of a Life of Muhammad, and had it printed at the expense of the Crown. He was unmasked, tried and imprisoned. Leonardo Sciascia later turned the affair into a novel.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Neuhaus, Advertissement pieux et très utile des Frères de la Rose-Croix (Paris, 1623)
stops.caption: Written when Paris was asking whether the Rosicrucian brotherhood existed at all. Eco kept it as a monument to a particular kind of reasoning.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

quote.text: It's about Neuhaus, the author of a tract on the Rosicrucian Order written in 1623, when the French were wondering whether or not the order had actually existed. 'The mere fact that they hid the fact of their existence is in itself proof that they existed,' says Neuhaus. The proof that they existed is that they denied existing.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco in conversation with Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2009; English translation 2011)

stops.title: Chassaignon, Cataractes de l'imagination (1779)
stops.caption: Four volumes whose full title promises a deluge of scribomania, a literary vomiting, an encyclopaedic haemorrhage and a monster of monsters. Eco quoted the title and left the contents to the imagination.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

quote.text: In 1779 the noble Mr Chassaignon wrote a four-volume work entitled Cataractes de l'imagination: déluge de la scribomanie, vomissement littéraire, hémorragie encyclopédique, monstre des monstres, whose content I shall leave to your imagination (it includes a tribute to the tribute, and a meditation on the roots of liquorice).
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco in conversation with Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2009; English translation 2011)

stops.title: Philomneste junior (Gustave Brunet), Les fous littéraires (Brussels, 1880)
stops.caption: A dictionary of literary madmen, in which the bibliographer Brunet made no distinction between crazy books and serious books by people who happened to be mad.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

quote.text: In Les Fous littéraires, Gustave Brunet does not distinguish between crazy books and serious books written by people who probably suffered from psychiatric problems. His delightful list of literary madmen includes Cyrano de Bergerac, Sade, Fourier, Newton, Poe and Whitman, but also Henrion, who in 1718 published an essay on Adam's vital statistics.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco in conversation with Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2009; English translation 2011)

stops.title: André Blavier, Les fous littéraires (1982)
stops.caption: A century after Brunet, the Belgian librarian Blavier catalogued the literary madmen, 1,500 works by Eco's count: new cosmogonies, the theology of the railway, proofs that the earth does not move.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

quote.text: In another book on literary madmen, André Blavier lists 1,500 works, whose authors include advocates of new cosmogonies, hygienists who recommend walking backwards, a certain Madrolle who explored the theology of the railway, a man called Passon who, in his 1829 work Démonstration de l'immobilité de la Terre, argued that the Earth doesn't move, and a Tardy who argued in 1878 that the Earth turns on its own axis every forty-eight hours.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco in conversation with Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2009; English translation 2011)

stops.title: Isaac de La Peyrère, Praeadamitae (1655)
stops.caption: The men before Adam: a Calvinist's argument that the Bible tells only the history of the Jews and that other peoples, the Chinese among them, are far older. The book was burned in Paris and its author made to recant before the Pope.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

quote.text: I'm thinking of the seventeenth-century French Protestant Isaac de La Peyrère's book Prae-Adamitae. It explains that the world is much older than the 6,000 years claimed in the Bible because Chinese ancestry can be traced back much further.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco in conversation with Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2009; English translation 2011)

stops.title: Charles Piazzi Smyth, Our Inheritance in the Great Pyramid (1864; this edition 1880)
stops.caption: The Astronomer Royal for Scotland measured the Great Pyramid and found in it the dimensions of the universe, the length of the year and a divine unit of length, the pyramid inch. Eco filed him with the men who believed their own language was Adam's.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

quote.text: Then there were the pyramidologists, the most famous of whom, the Scottish astronomer Charles Piazzi Smyth, found all the dimensions of the universe in the Giza pyramid. It's still an extremely active field, which these days operates predominantly online.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco in conversation with Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2009; English translation 2011)

image.alt: A plate from Piazzi Smyth's Our Inheritance in the Great Pyramid (1864)

stops.title: Ignatius Donnelly, The Great Cryptogram (1888)
stops.caption: A Minnesota congressman proves, nearly a thousand pages of number-counting, that Francis Bacon wrote Shakespeare and hid the confession in the plays as a cipher. The shelf around it holds the whole Baconian library: Theobald's Shakespeare studies in Baconian light stands next door.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Eugène Aroux, Preuves de l'hérésie de Dante (1857)
stops.caption: Proofs that Dante was a heretic: Aroux, following Gabriele Rossetti, read the Comedy as a coded manifesto of a secret sect. Eco made this school of reading his textbook case of overinterpretation.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

quote.text: Rossetti sets out with the conviction that Dante was a Freemason, Templar, and member of the Fraternity of the Rosy Cross, and he therefore assumes that a Masonic-Rosicrucian symbol would be as follows: a rose with the cross inside it, under which appears a pelican … Rossetti's tragedy is that he does not find in Dante any remarkable analogy with Masonic symbology.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, 'Interpretation and Overinterpretation', Tanner Lectures at Clare Hall, Cambridge (1990)

stops.title: Dr Bataille (Léo Taxil), Le diable au XIXe siècle (Paris, 1892 to 1894)
stops.caption: Two illustrated volumes of devil-worship inside Freemasonry, with the confessions of the high priestess Diana Vaughan. In 1897 Taxil announced to a packed hall in Paris that he had invented all of it. He is a character in The Prague Cemetery.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

image.alt: An illustrated page from Le diable au XIXe siècle (1892)

stops.title: Cesare Lombroso, L'uomo delinquente (1876; this edition 1924)
stops.caption: The criminal man: the Turin doctor who taught that criminals are born, and can be recognised by the shape of the skull and the ears. Science that was wrong, in Eco's phrase, and a direct descendant of the physiognomy books on the shelf beside it.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Johann Caspar Lavater, Physiognomische Fragmente (1775 to 1778; this edition 1783)
stops.caption: Lavater's four volumes taught Europe to read virtue and vice in profiles, and made silhouettes a craze. Goethe helped with the first volume and later disowned the enterprise.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Louis Jacolliot, Le vere origini della Bibbia (Italian edition)
stops.caption: A French colonial judge in India claimed that the Bible had been copied from Hindu scriptures and Christ from a god called Christna. His books fed the occult India of the theosophists, and the underground kingdom of Agartha.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Saint-Yves d'Alveydre, Mission des juifs (1884)
stops.caption: Saint-Yves set out in this book the synarchy, a government of co-operating powers that he offered as the cure for class war, and in the book that followed, Mission de l'Inde en Europe, gave it a hidden capital, Agartha beneath the Himalayas. The Synarchy is one of the conspiracies the three editors of Foucault's Pendulum feed into their Plan.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: I Protocolli dei Savi anziani di Sion (1938)
stops.caption: A Fascist-era Italian edition of the most murderous forgery in history, the minutes of a Jewish world conspiracy assembled from a French satire and a German novel. Eco traced its making in essays and then in The Prague Cemetery.

source.label: Umberto Eco, The Prague Cemetery (2010)

quote.text: From lies to forgeries the step is not so long, and I have written technical essays on the logic of forgeries and on the influence of forgeries on history. The most famous and terrible of those forgeries is the Protocols.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, interviewed by Stephen Moss, The Guardian (27 November 2011)

image.alt: Title page of Nilus's Velikoe v malom (1905), which printed the Protocols

stops.title: Umberto Eco, I limiti dell'interpretazione (1990)
stops.caption: Where the collection turns back into theory: the book in which Eco set out what he called a theory of fakes and forgeries, and explained why a library of error belongs to a scholar of truth.

source.label: Umberto Eco, The Limits of Interpretation (1990)

quote.text: I am fascinated by error, by bad faith and idiocy. Like Flaubert. You and I both adore silliness. In Faith in Fakes I describe visiting American museums that show reproductions of art works, including a waxwork Venus de Milo with arms. In The Limits of Interpretation I create a theory of fakes and forgeries.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco in conversation with Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2009; English translation 2011)

tours.title: Lists, encyclopaedias and the vertigo of the whole
tours.blurb: Eco said that culture begins with the list: Homer's catalogue of ships, the saints, the medicinal plants, the professions of the world. This tour walks the shelves where the collection tries to hold everything, from Pliny to the first atlas, and ends with the arts of memory.

stops.title: Umberto Eco, Vertigine della lista (2009)
stops.caption: The book of lists Eco wrote for the Louvre, from the shield of Achilles to Joyce, with an argument about why we make them.

source.label: Umberto Eco, The Infinity of Lists (2009)

quote.text: We have a limit, a very discouraging, humiliating limit: death. That's why we like all the things that we assume have no limits and, therefore, no end. It's a way of escaping thoughts about death. We like lists because we don't want to die.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, interviewed by Der Spiegel, 'We Like Lists Because We Don't Want to Die' (2009)

stops.title: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis historia (Venice, 1487)
stops.caption: Thirty-seven books of everything the Romans knew, or thought they knew: 20,000 facts from 2,000 volumes, by Pliny's own count, arranged as a vast list from the stars down to the gemstones. Eco traced the first list of all to Homer.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

quote.text: La lista mi ha sempre affascinato. Ha la lista qualche cosa a che vedere con la memoria? Ma sì, perché è un modo di raccogliere tutto quello che si sapeva a proposito di qualcosa senza essere obbligati ad organizzarlo. Il primo elenco comincia col catalogo delle navi nell'Iliade.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, in Davide Ferrario's Sulla memoria, part 3 (Venice Biennale, 2015)
quote.translation: The list has always fascinated me. Does the list have something to do with memory? Well yes, because it is a way of gathering everything that was known about something without being obliged to organise it. The first list begins with the catalogue of ships in the Iliad.

image.credit: Pliny the Elder (text), printed by Johannes de Spira, Venice, 1469
image.alt: A page of the first printed Pliny, Venice 1469

stops.title: Solinus, Polyhistor (Basel, 1543)
stops.caption: The collector of marvels: Solinus boiled Pliny down to the wonders, the dog-headed men and the fountains that cure, and his digest was copied for a thousand years. Most of the monsters at the edges of medieval maps came from him.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Isidore of Seville, Etymologiae (Strasbourg, about 1473)
stops.caption: The encyclopaedia of the early Middle Ages, which explains every thing by the origin of its name, usually wrongly and always memorably. Eco's blind librarian Jorge would have known it by heart.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Bartholomaeus Anglicus, De proprietatibus rerum (1480)
stops.caption: On the properties of things: a Franciscan's nineteen books on God, angels, the body, the animals and the colours, the reference work of the thirteenth century and one of the models for the library in The Name of the Rose.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Vincent of Beauvais, Speculum doctrinale (1494)
stops.caption: One part of the Great Mirror, the largest encyclopaedia of the Middle Ages, assembled by a Dominican for Louis IX. Vincent had no view of his own; he cut and pasted everything anyone had written.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Werner Rolevinck, Fasciculus temporum (1490)
stops.caption: A bundle of times: the first printed timeline, with the history of the world running as a double line down the page, popes above and emperors below, and small woodcuts of cities and marvels along the way.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Jacopo Filippo Foresti, Supplementum chronicarum (Venice, 1513)
stops.caption: An Augustinian friar's chronicle of the world from Creation to his own day, reprinted and extended for decades. Every printer who owned it added a few more years.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Hartmann Schedel, the Nuremberg Chronicle (1493)
stops.caption: The chronicle's map of the known world, with the monstrous races down its margin, was the picture of everything for the generation before Columbus's discoveries were understood.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

quote.text: And now, to reply to your question, I only possess about thirty incunabula, though they do include what you might call the 'essentials'. For instance, the Hypnerotomachia Poliphili, the Nuremberg Chronicle, Ficino's translation of the Corpus Hermeticum, the Arbor Vitae Crucifixae Jesu Christi by Ubertino Da Casale (who became one of the characters in my Name of the Rose), and so on.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco in conversation with Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2009; English translation 2011)

image.alt: The world map from the Nuremberg Chronicle (1493)

stops.title: Abraham Ortelius, Theatrum orbis terrarum (Antwerp, 1575)
stops.caption: The first modern atlas: the whole world as a set of uniform maps, one per country, bound in a single volume. The Theatre of the World was the list of places, and it still shows the great southern continent that nobody had found.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

image.alt: The world map from Ortelius's Theatrum orbis terrarum

stops.title: Conrad Gesner, Mithridates (1555; this edition 1610)
stops.caption: A list of all the languages of the world, with the Lord's Prayer in twenty-two of them, by the Swiss naturalist who also tried to list every animal and every book ever printed.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Tommaso Garzoni, La piazza universale di tutte le professioni del mondo (Venice, 1599)
stops.caption: The universal square of all the professions of the world: 155 discourses on everything from theologians to charlatans, pimps and fools. Garzoni also wrote a hospital of incurable madmen and a theatre of the world's brains.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Jean-Jacques Boissard, Theatrum vitae humanae (Metz, 1596)
stops.caption: The theatre of human life in emblems, engraved by Theodor de Bry: the ages of man, the vices, the fortunes, each with a picture and a moral, the whole of life as an illustrated index.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Petrus de Natalibus, Catalogus sanctorum (1545)
stops.caption: The catalogue of the saints, arranged by the calendar, with a life for every day. Eco put the lists of saints beside the lists of armies and medicinal plants as the raw material of culture.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

quote.text: The list doesn't destroy culture; it creates it. Wherever you look in cultural history, you will find lists. In fact, there is a dizzying array: lists of saints, armies and medicinal plants, or of treasures and book titles. Think of the nature collections of the 16th century. My novels, by the way, are full of lists.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, interviewed by Der Spiegel, 'We Like Lists Because We Don't Want to Die' (2009)

stops.title: John Wilkins, An Essay towards a Real Character and a Philosophical Language (London, 1668)
stops.caption: A bishop of the Royal Society divides everything in the universe into forty categories and gives each thing a written sign built from its place in the table: the most ambitious list ever attempted, and Borges's favourite failure.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

quote.text: The other one, less famous, was John Wilkins, who in his Essay Toward a Real Character (1668), tried to build the perfect language envisaged by some of his contemporaries, like Mersenne, Guldin and others. … As I tried to explain it in my book The Search for the Perfect Language (1993), Wilkins' project was impracticable.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, 'Between La Mancha and Babel', Variaciones Borges 4 (1997)

image.alt: Title page of Wilkins's Essay towards a Real Character (1668)

stops.title: François Rabelais, Oeuvres (Amsterdam, 1741)
stops.caption: The catalogue of the library of Saint-Victor in Pantagruel is the great comic list of literature: 139 imaginary titles in its final form, from the Codpiece of the Law to the Art of Farting Politely in Company. Eco recited it as a litany.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

quote.text: We remain, nostalgic and curious to know what those volumes were about, and savouring the pleasure of repeating their names like in a litany: Bragheta juris, De babuinis et scimiis cum commento Dorbellis, Ars honeste petandi in societate, Formicarium Artium, De modo cacandi.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, 'Between La Mancha and Babel', Variaciones Borges 4 (1997)

image.credit: Gustave Dore, illustration for Rabelais's Gargantua et Pantagruel (19th-century illustrated edition)
image.alt: Gustave Doré's engraving for the prologue of Gargantua

stops.title: Cicero, De oratore (1559)
stops.caption: Where the art of memory begins: Cicero tells how the poet Simonides identified the crushed guests of a collapsed banquet hall by remembering where each had sat. Every memory palace since, including the abbey library of The Name of the Rose, descends from that story.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

quote.text: In his De oratore, Cicero describes Simonides attending a dinner with many of Greece's senior dignitaries. At a certain point in the evening, Simonides takes a break from the gathering, only for the ceiling to collapse and all the other guests to be killed. Simonides is called in to identify the bodies. He manages to do this by remembering each person's place at the table.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco in conversation with Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2009; English translation 2011)

stops.title: Johannes Romberch, Congestorium artificiosae memoriae (Venice, 1520)
stops.caption: A Dominican's handbook of artificial memory, with woodcuts of the alphabets of things and the imaginary buildings in which a preacher stored his sermons. Memory here is a list with a floor plan.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Giulio Camillo, L'idea del theatro (Florence, 1550)
stops.caption: Camillo built a wooden theatre in which the spectator stood on the stage and the whole of knowledge was arranged in the seats, and promised the King of France it would let anyone speak on any subject like Cicero. This is the description he left of it.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Umberto Eco, Dall'albero al labirinto (2007)
stops.caption: From the tree to the labyrinth: Eco's own history of how the West tried to organise knowledge, and why the dictionary always turns back into an encyclopaedia. In Davide Ferrario's film he also says what a memory must do to stay sane.

source.label: Umberto Eco, From the Tree to the Labyrinth (2007)

quote.text: Quindi qual è la seconda virtù della memoria? La prima è quella che conserva, la seconda è quella che filtra. Guai se la memoria, sia individuale che collettiva, non facesse delle decimazioni giorno per giorno, buttasse via quello che non vale la pena.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, in Davide Ferrario's film Umberto Eco: La biblioteca del mondo (2022)
quote.translation: So what is the second virtue of memory? The first is the one that preserves, the second is the one that filters. Woe if memory, individual as well as collective, did not carry out decimations day by day, throwing away what is not worth keeping.

tours.title: Imaginary lands and voyages
tours.blurb: Eco's last illustrated book was a history of legendary lands: the flat earth, the earthly paradise, the kingdom of Prester John, Atlantis, the moon. Most of the books it drew on are here. This tour sails from a sixth-century world in a box to a nineteenth-century Atlantis.

stops.title: Umberto Eco, Storia delle terre e dei luoghi leggendari (2013)
stops.caption: The book of legendary lands, Eco's illustrated history of the places people believed in and looked for: lands that never existed but changed the geography of the ones that did.

source.label: Umberto Eco, The Book of Legendary Lands (2013)

stops.title: Cosmas Indicopleustes, Christian Topography
stops.caption: A sixth-century merchant turned monk who argued that the earth is a flat rectangle under a vaulted heaven, shaped like the tabernacle of Moses. Almost nobody in the Middle Ages believed him; the flat earth, Eco showed, is mostly a modern legend about the past.

source.label: Biblioteca Universitaria di Bologna, the record of Eco's copy

image.alt: The world as a box under the vault of heaven, from Cosmas Indicopleustes

stops.title: Sir John Mandeville, Travels
stops.caption: The most popular travel book of the Middle Ages, by a knight who probably never left his library. Mandeville visits Prester John, the men whose heads grow beneath their shoulders and the fountain of youth, and Columbus carried him in his head.

source.label: Biblioteca Universitaria di Bologna, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: The Letter of Prester John
stops.caption: The letter that invented a Christian empire in the East and kept explorers searching for it from Asia to Ethiopia. Eco gave it a forger in Baudolino.

source.label: Umberto Eco, Baudolino (2000)

quote.text: Molti documenti falsi hanno però provocato dei grandi avvenimenti storici, la donazione di Costantino, la lettera del Prete Gianni che ha spinto all'esplorazione prima dell'Asia e poi dell'Africa.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, in Davide Ferrario's film Umberto Eco: La biblioteca del mondo (2022)
quote.translation: Many forged documents have provoked great historical events: the Donation of Constantine, the letter of Prester John which drove the exploration first of Asia and then of Africa.

stops.title: Benedetto Bordone, Isolario (Venice, 1534)
stops.caption: A book of islands, real and otherwise: Venice, Cuba, Japan and the isles of the Ocean, each with its own woodcut map. The isolario is the form Eco's Island of the Day Before belongs to.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

image.alt: Title page of Bordone's Isolario (1528 edition)

stops.title: Giovanni Battista Ramusio, Delle navigationi et viaggi (Venice, 1606)
stops.caption: The great Venetian collection of voyages, Marco Polo beside Columbus and the Portuguese, the moment the imaginary geography of the Middle Ages met the reports of people who had actually been there.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Joseph Hall, Mundus alter et idem (1605; this edition 1643)
stops.caption: Another world and yet the same: a satirical voyage to the southern continent, whose provinces are Crapulia, Viraginia, Moronia and Lavernia, the lands of gluttons, of nagging women, of fools and of thieves, with a map. Eco's collection of imaginary lands is also a collection of satires on the real one.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Francis Godwin, L'homme dans la lune (Paris, 1648)
stops.caption: The first English voyage to the moon, in French: a Spaniard is carried there by a flock of trained geese and finds a Christian utopia. Cyrano read it, and so did every later moon voyager.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

image.alt: Title page of Godwin's The Man in the Moone (1638)

stops.title: John Wilkins, The Discovery of a World in the Moone (1638)
stops.caption: The same Wilkins who invented a philosophical language argued, at twenty-four, that the moon is a world with seas and inhabitants, and that one day we would find a way to fly there.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Cyrano de Bergerac, L'altro mondo
stops.caption: The states and empires of the moon, reached by bottles of dew and by rocket. Cyrano's moon has cities on wheels and is governed by philosophers who find the earth ridiculous. Brunet listed him among the literary madmen; Eco listed him among the essentials.

source.label: Biblioteca Universitaria di Bologna, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Francis Bacon, La nouvelle Atlantide (1702)
stops.caption: Bacon's island of Bensalem, where the house of Salomon runs the world's first research institute. Eco was doubtful about utopias that might actually be built.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

quote.text: If the utopia of Thomas More were ever realized, I have little doubt it would be a Stalinist society.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, interviewed by Lila Azam Zanganeh, The Paris Review, 'The Art of Fiction No. 197' (2008)

stops.title: Denis Veiras, Histoire des Sévarambes (1677 to 1679; this edition 1716)
stops.caption: The history of a people in the southern land, ruled by sun-worshipping wise men, told as the true report of a shipwrecked captain. Readers argued for years about whether the Sévarambes existed.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Voyages imaginaires, songes, visions et romans cabalistiques (1787 to 1789; this volume 1788)
stops.caption: Thirty-six volumes in which the publisher Garnier gathered every imaginary voyage he could find, from Gulliver to the underground world of Holberg. The set is the eighteenth century's own map of legendary lands.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Pierre-Daniel Huet, Traité de la situation du paradis terrestre (1691; this edition 1701)
stops.caption: The learned bishop of Avranches locates the Garden of Eden precisely, at the junction of the Tigris and the Euphrates, with a map. The search for the earthly paradise takes up a chapter of Eco's book of legendary lands.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Athanasius Kircher, Mundus subterraneus (Amsterdam, 1664 to 1665)
stops.caption: Kircher's map of Atlantis, drawn with south at the top, is the first map of the island anyone had made, and the one every later Atlantis book copied.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

image.alt: Kircher's map of Atlantis in the middle of the Atlantic, from Mundus subterraneus

stops.title: Jean-Sylvain Bailly, Lettres sur l'Atlantide de Platon (1779)
stops.caption: The astronomer who became mayor of Paris during the Revolution argued that Atlantis lay in the Arctic, near Spitsbergen, and that all science had come from the north. He was guillotined in 1793.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Ignatius Donnelly, Atlantis: the Antediluvian World (1882; this edition 1910)
stops.caption: The book that made Atlantis modern: the same Donnelly who found Bacon's cipher in Shakespeare made the sunken continent the source of every civilisation, and drew it a map.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

image.alt: Donnelly's map of Atlantis (1882)

stops.title: Walter de la Mare, Desert Islands and Robinson Crusoe (1930)
stops.caption: A poet's anthology of the desert island in literature, from Crusoe backwards. Eco shelved it with the imaginary voyages; the island that nobody can reach is the subject of his third novel.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: L. Sprague de Camp and Willy Ley, Le terre leggendarie
stops.caption: Atlantis, the wanderings of Odysseus, Prester John's kingdom and El Dorado, examined by a science-fiction writer and a science writer with a taste for debunking: the Italian translation of Lands Beyond. A working copy for Eco's own book on the same lands.

source.label: Biblioteca Universitaria di Bologna, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Françoise de Graffigny, Lettres d'une Péruvienne (1747; this edition 1752)
stops.caption: The bestselling novel of an Inca princess carried off to France, whose letters home are written in knotted cords. Eco kept it for the book it provoked: a Neapolitan prince's treatise on the quipu, standing in the rare room.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

quote.text: In the eighteenth century, Madame de Graffigny wrote the hugely successful novel Letters from a Peruvian Woman. The Neapolitan prince and alchemist Raimondo di Sangro studied Mme de Graffigny's book in great depth and produced that wonderful illustrated book about quipus.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco in conversation with Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2009; English translation 2011)

tours.title: Eco and the comics
tours.blurb: Eco read comics before he could read, wrote his own as a boy, and in 1964 was the first Italian professor to take Superman and Charlie Brown seriously in print. He co-founded the magazine Linus and collected the strips of the 1930s all his life. This tour visits the comics shelves and the books he wrote about them.

stops.title: Umberto Eco, Apocalittici e integrati (1964)
stops.caption: The book that brought comics into the university: essays on Superman, on Steve Canyon and on Charlie Brown, written by a thirty-two-year-old who refused to choose between Joyce and the funny pages. The Superman essay explains why the hero must never really change.

source.label: Umberto Eco, Apocalypse Postponed (essays from Apocalittici e integrati, 1964)

quote.text: The taste for the iterative scheme is presented then as a taste for redundance. The hunger for entertaining narrative based on these mechanisms is a hunger for redundance. … It is not a matter of discovering who committed the crime, but, rather, of following certain 'topical' gestures of 'topical' characters whose stock behavior we already love.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, 'The Myth of Superman', translated by Natalie Chilton, Diacritics 2, no. 1 (1972); from 'Il mito di Superman' (1962), collected in Apocalittici e integrati (1964)

stops.title: Linus, the magazine (from 1965)
stops.caption: The Italian comics monthly named after Linus van Pelt, which opened its first issue in April 1965 with Eco, Elio Vittorini and Oreste del Buono discussing Peanuts. Eco's 1963 introduction to Charlie Brown is the classic statement of why the strip mattered.

source.label: Linus, first issue, April 1965 (Milano Libri)

quote.text: Charlie Brown: ingenuous, stubborn, always awkward, and doomed to failure. … His solitude becomes an abyss, his inferiority complex is pervasive—tinged by the constant suspicion (which the reader also comes to share) that Charlie Brown is not inferior. Worse: he is absolutely normal.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, 'On Krazy Kat and Peanuts', The New York Review of Books (13 June 1985; from Apocalittici e integrati, 1964)

stops.title: Linus, the Eco issue
stops.caption: Linus marked Eco's death in 2016 with a back cover drawn as a tribute, Eco as Superman, as Charlie Brown, as a Smurf, and a strip inside. His daughter Carlotta shows it in Davide Ferrario's film.

source.label: Carlotta Eco in Davide Ferrario's film Umberto Eco: La biblioteca del mondo (2022)

quote.text: Ti ricordi questo numero di Linus che hanno fatto una controcopertina, cioè lui vestito da Superman, da Charlie Brown, da Puffo … E poi c'era dentro un fumetto che racconta la storia di come lui guarda dal balconcino praticamente il funerale, e si commuove.
quote.attribution: Carlotta Eco, in Davide Ferrario's film Umberto Eco: La biblioteca del mondo (2022)
quote.translation: Do you remember this issue of Linus? They did a back cover with him dressed as Superman, as Charlie Brown, as a Smurf. And inside there was a comic strip telling the story of how he watches, more or less, his own funeral from the little balcony, and is moved.

stops.title: Corriere dei Piccoli
stops.caption: The children's weekly of the Corriere della Sera, founded in 1908, which printed American strips with the balloons removed and rhyming couplets underneath. It is the paper the amnesiac hero of The Mysterious Flame of Queen Loana finds in the attic, and the one Eco read as a boy.

source.label: askanews, 'I libri e lo Studiolo di Umberto Eco, meraviglie alla Braidense' (5 May 2022)

image.alt: Cover of the first Corriere dei Piccoli, 27 December 1908

stops.title: Topolino giornalista
stops.caption: The 1930s Italian album of the Mickey Mouse strip in which Mickey runs a newspaper, one of the childhood comics Eco gave back to Yambo, the bookseller who has lost his memory in The Mysterious Flame of Queen Loana.

source.label: askanews, 'I libri e lo Studiolo di Umberto Eco, meraviglie alla Braidense' (5 May 2022)

stops.title: Alex Raymond, Flash Gordon
stops.caption: Flash Gordon on the planet Mongo, fighting the tyrant Ming: in The Mysterious Flame of Queen Loana Eco makes him the hero who taught an Italian boy under Fascism what a fight for freedom looked like. Eco also noted, as a collector, what an original Raymond page costs today.

source.label: Biblioteca Universitaria di Bologna, the record of Eco's copy

quote.text: If you want to buy an original of one of the great comic strips, it is horribly expensive, because they are so rare (these days, a single page of Alex Raymond's work costs a fortune). But why are they so rare? Simply because the newspapers that used to publish them threw the plates in the bin the moment the strip had been printed.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco in conversation with Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2009; English translation 2011)

stops.title: E. C. Segar, Braccio di Ferro (Popeye)
stops.caption: Popeye, who first walked into Segar's Thimble Theatre in January 1929 and took it over. Eco described himself as a fan and collector of the strips of the 1930s, and Popeye is one of them.

source.label: Biblioteca Universitaria di Bologna, the record of Eco's copy

quote.text: As a fan and collector of 1930s comic strips, I find it quite impossible to read contemporary graphic novels, or at least the most avant-garde. But it's important not to bury one's head in the sand.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco in conversation with Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2009; English translation 2011)

image.alt: Popeye's first appearance in Thimble Theatre, 17 January 1929

stops.title: Lee Falk, Mandrake
stops.caption: Mandrake the Magician, the top-hatted hypnotist of 1934, in the pile with the other albums of Eco's childhood.

source.label: askanews, 'I libri e lo Studiolo di Umberto Eco, meraviglie alla Braidense' (5 May 2022)

stops.title: Lee Falk, L'Uomo Mascherato (The Phantom)
stops.caption: The Phantom, the ghost who walks, chasing Diana Palmer through the jungle of Bengalla. Eco counted the Phantom's adventures among the memories he had stolen from books, which he said had given him a very long childhood.

source.label: Umberto Eco: La biblioteca del mondo (Davide Ferrario, 2022)

quote.text: Ho la sensazione di aver avuto un'infanzia lunghissima e piena proprio perché è piena di ricordi che ho rubato ad altri: li ho rubati a Sandokan e Yanez mentre correvano coi loro prao i mari malesi, a D'Artagnan mentre duellava con il barone Winter, all'Uomo Mascherato che inseguiva Diana Palmer, e anche a Renzo e Lucia in fuga sul ramo di Como.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, in Davide Ferrario's film Umberto Eco: La biblioteca del mondo (2022)
quote.translation: I have the feeling of having had a very long and full childhood, precisely because it is full of memories I stole from others: I stole them from Sandokan and Yanez racing their praus across the Malay seas, from d'Artagnan duelling with Baron Winter, from the Phantom chasing Diana Palmer, and from Renzo and Lucia too, fleeing along the Como branch of the lake.

stops.title: Tex Willer
stops.caption: The Bonelli western that has run since 1948, the longest-lived Italian comic. Eco kept the studies of it with the strips themselves.

source.label: Biblioteca Universitaria di Bologna, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Gianni Brunoro, Corto come un romanzo
stops.caption: A study of Hugo Pratt's sailor Corto Maltese, the most literary of Italian comics heroes. Eco's often-repeated line about Pratt turned the usual snobbery inside out.

source.label: Biblioteca Universitaria di Bologna, the record of Eco's copy

quote.text: Quando ho voglia di rilassarmi leggo un saggio di Engels, se invece desidero impegnarmi leggo Corto Maltese.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, as quoted by Marco Pellitteri, 'La nona arte secondo Umberto Eco', doppiozero (2019)
quote.translation: When I want to relax I read an essay by Engels; when instead I want something demanding I read Corto Maltese.

stops.title: Guido Crepax: Valentina, la forma del tempo
stops.caption: Crepax's Valentina, the Milan photographer with the Louise Brooks bob who first appeared in Linus in 1965, in the catalogue of a 2008 exhibition. Crepax and Eco belonged to the same Milan of the 1960s, and Linus was where they met on the page.

source.label: Biblioteca Universitaria di Bologna, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Jules Feiffer, Il complesso facile
stops.caption: The Village Voice cartoonist's anxious New Yorkers, in Italian, from 1962: the kind of adult comic strip Linus was founded to publish three years later.

source.label: Biblioteca Universitaria di Bologna, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Bonvi, Fall-out fall-out fall-out
stops.caption: Bonvi, the creator of the Sturmtruppen, on life after the bomb. The Italian comic of the 1970s and 1980s, from Linus to the satirical weeklies, is shelved here in the living room.

source.label: Biblioteca Universitaria di Bologna, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Nuvole maliziose: fumetti e peccati capitali
stops.caption: Comics and the seven deadly sins, an anthology from 1985. The living-room shelves mix the strips with the books that take them apart.

source.label: Biblioteca Universitaria di Bologna, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Annie Baron-Carvais, La bande dessinée
stops.caption: A pocket history of the comic strip in the Que sais-je? series, from the Yellow Kid of 1895 onwards. Eco's own history of the medium was written a generation earlier, essay by essay.

source.label: Biblioteca Universitaria di Bologna, the record of Eco's copy

image.alt: The Yellow Kid by R. F. Outcault (1897)

stops.title: Bertrand Portevin, Le monde inconnu d'Hergé
stops.caption: A study of the hidden world of Tintin's creator. Hergé's clear line belongs to the same 1930s that produced Eco's favourite American strips.

source.label: Biblioteca Universitaria di Bologna, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: I fumetti di Mao (1971)
stops.caption: Chinese comics of the Cultural Revolution, collected by a journalist in China, with essays by Eco and the sinologist Jean Chesneaux. Eco later remembered how little the comics revealed of what was actually happening.

source.label: Umberto Eco, introduction to I fumetti di Mao (1971)

quote.text: In 1971 I contributed to a book about Chinese comics. A journalist based in China had collected together all kinds of material: comic books in the English style, but also photo stories. The comics had been created during the Cultural Revolution, but they gave no indication whatsoever of what was happening in China at the time.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco in conversation with Jean-Claude Carrière, This Is Not the End of the Book (2009; English translation 2011)

stops.title: Storia del racconto popolare: prima del fumetto
stops.caption: A history of popular storytelling before the comic strip, from the broadsheet ballad to the illustrated feuilleton, shelved where the serial novels turn into comics.

source.label: Umberto Eco: La biblioteca del mondo (Davide Ferrario, 2022)

stops.title: Umberto Eco, La bustina di Minerva (2000)
stops.caption: Fifteen years of Eco's back-page column in L'Espresso, named after the matchbook he jotted ideas on. The column of June 1991 explained why reading lengthens life.

source.label: Umberto Eco, La bustina di Minerva (2000)

quote.text: Il libro è un'assicurazione sulla vita, una piccola anticipazione di immortalità. All'indietro (ahimé) anziché in avanti.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, 'Perché i libri allungano la vita', La bustina di Minerva, L'Espresso (2 June 1991)
quote.translation: The book is a life-insurance policy, a small advance on immortality. Backwards, alas, rather than forwards.

tours.title: Feuilletons and the pleasures of popular fiction
tours.blurb: Eco's first books were the unbound serial novels in his grandfather's box: Dumas, Sue, Salgari. He read them all his life, wrote a book about their supermen, and built The Prague Cemetery out of their engravings. This tour runs along the shelves of popular fiction in the corridor and living room.

stops.title: Umberto Eco, Il superuomo di massa (1976)
stops.caption: The superman of the masses: Eco's book on the heroes of the popular novel, from Sue's Rodolphe and Dumas's Monte Cristo to James Bond, and on the consolations these books provide.

source.label: Umberto Eco, Il superuomo di massa (1976; enlarged 1978)

quote.text: Metterà in opera una tale energia, sprigionerà una tale felicità, se non inventiva almeno combinatoria, da procurare piaceri che sarebbe ipocrita nascondere.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, Il superuomo di massa (1978)
quote.translation: It will set in motion such energy, will release such happiness, if not inventive then at least combinatory, as to procure pleasures it would be hypocritical to hide.

stops.title: Emilio Salgari, Le Tigri di Mompracem
stops.caption: Sandokan, the Tiger of Malaysia, and his Portuguese friend Yanez, on the prau against the British of Labuan. Salgari never left Italy; Eco, who read him as a boy in wartime, said the memories were his own.

source.label: Umberto Eco: La biblioteca del mondo (Davide Ferrario, 2022)

quote.text: Ho la sensazione di aver avuto un'infanzia lunghissima e piena proprio perché è piena di ricordi che ho rubato ad altri: li ho rubati a Sandokan e Yanez mentre correvano coi loro prao i mari malesi.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, in Davide Ferrario's film Umberto Eco: La biblioteca del mondo (2022)
quote.translation: I have the feeling of having had a very long and full childhood, precisely because it is full of memories I stole from others: I stole them from Sandokan and Yanez racing their praus across the Malay seas.

image.credit: Alberto della Valle (1851-1928), cover for the 1906 edition
image.alt: Cover of Salgari's Le Tigri di Mompracem, 1906 edition

stops.title: Emilio Salgari, Il Corsaro Nero
stops.caption: The Black Corsair, the Ligurian count turned Caribbean pirate, sworn to avenge his brothers. The row of Salgari in the living room holds the pirate cycle beside the Malaysian one.

source.label: Umberto Eco: La biblioteca del mondo (Davide Ferrario, 2022)

stops.title: Emilio Salgari, I misteri della jungla nera
stops.caption: Tremal-Naik, the hunter of the Black Jungle, against the Thugs of Kali: the first of the Indian novels and the book that introduced the villain Suyodhana. Eco defended exactly this kind of reading.

source.label: Umberto Eco: La biblioteca del mondo (Davide Ferrario, 2022)

quote.text: Quel tanto di vita che si conquista leggendo non discrimina tra grandi opere d'arte e letteratura di trattenimento: non fatevi ricattare da chi vi dice che bisogna leggere solo i libri importanti.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, in Davide Ferrario's film Umberto Eco: La biblioteca del mondo (2022)
quote.translation: The extra life one gains by reading does not discriminate between great works of art and entertainment literature: don't let yourselves be blackmailed by those who tell you that one must read only important books.

stops.title: Souvestre and Allain, Fantômas
stops.caption: The genius of crime in evening dress and a mask, thirty-two volumes written at speed between 1911 and 1913, adored by the surrealists and by every reader of the feuilleton. The first cover, with Fantômas striding over Paris, became the image of the whole series.

source.label: Umberto Eco: La biblioteca del mondo (Davide Ferrario, 2022)

image.alt: Cover of the first Fantômas (1911)

stops.title: Carlo Collodi, Pinocchio
stops.caption: The puppet who lies and grows a longer nose each time is a natural subject for a theorist of lying. Eco wrote the introduction to Geoffrey Brock's English Pinocchio in 2009, and once, with his students, rewrote the story with every word beginning with P.

source.label: Umberto Eco: La biblioteca del mondo (Davide Ferrario, 2022)

image.alt: Enrico Mazzanti's Pinocchio (1883)

stops.title: Vamba, Il giornalino di Gian Burrasca
stops.caption: The diary of Giannino Stoppani, the nine-year-old terror of his household, from 1912: the funniest book of Italian childhood, shelved in the corridor with the other boyhood classics.

source.label: Umberto Eco: La biblioteca del mondo (Davide Ferrario, 2022)

stops.title: Alexandre Dumas, Il conte di Montecristo
stops.caption: Eco's favourite badly written masterpiece. His essay in praise of Monte Cristo argues that the novel is gripping in spite of its prose, and admits that he once tried to translate it into better Italian and gave up.

source.label: Umberto Eco, 'Elogio del Montecristo' (1985)

quote.text: Montecristo è uno dei romanzi più appassionanti che mai siano stati scritti. In un colpo solo … riesce a inscatolare nello stesso romanzo tre situazioni archetipe capaci di torcere le viscere anche a un boia.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, 'Elogio del Montecristo', in Sugli specchi e altri saggi (1985); text as reproduced on the blog Salvatore Lo Leggio (2012)
quote.translation: Monte Cristo is one of the most gripping novels ever written. In a single stroke it manages to pack into one novel three archetypal situations capable of wringing the guts even of an executioner.

stops.title: Mémoires de M. d'Artagnan (Cologne, 1700)
stops.caption: The pseudo-memoirs by Courtilz de Sandras from which Dumas took d'Artagnan and the three musketeers. Eco kept the source in the rare room and the novels in the corridor. The first books he ever saw were his grandfather's unbound Dumas.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

quote.text: So he had a lot of unbound books lying here and there around his apartment—old, beautifully illustrated editions of popular nineteenth-century novels by Gautier and Dumas. Those were the first books I ever saw.
quote.attribution: Umberto Eco, interviewed by Lila Azam Zanganeh, The Paris Review, 'The Art of Fiction No. 197' (2008)

stops.title: Alexandre Dumas, Ascanio
stops.caption: Dumas's novel of Benvenuto Cellini at the court of Francis I, from the years of the Musketeers. The shelf is a run of Dumas in nineteenth-century illustrated editions, the kind whose engravings Eco reused in The Prague Cemetery.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Eugène Sue, Le Juif errant (1844 to 1845)
stops.caption: The Wandering Jew, Sue's serial about a Jesuit plot to seize an inheritance, illustrated by Louis Huard. Its picture of a Jesuit world conspiracy was one of the fictions that fed the Protocols, which is why it matters so much in The Prague Cemetery.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

image.alt: Gavarni's illustration for Sue's Le Juif errant (1844 to 1845)

stops.title: Eugène Sue, Les mystères de Paris
stops.caption: The first great feuilleton, 1842 to 1843: Prince Rodolphe in disguise among the poor of Paris, the model of every serial that followed. Eco's Superuomo di massa returns to it and defends the pleasure such novels give.

source.label: Biblioteca Universitaria di Bologna, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Xavier de Montépin, Sa Majesté l'Argent
stops.caption: Montépin, the most prolific of the feuilletonists, with a novel on the majesty of money. The shelf of feuilletons is where Eco's Superuomo di massa was researched: the popular novelist as a manufacturer of consolation.

source.label: Biblioteca Nazionale Braidense, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Ponson du Terrail, le romancier à la plume infatigable
stops.caption: A life of the inventor of Rocambole, the hero whose adventures were so improbable that his name became a French word. Ponson wrote several serials at once and was said to have killed a character in one paper while he went on talking in another.

source.label: Biblioteca Universitaria di Bologna, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Carolina Invernizio, Matilde Serao, Liala
stops.caption: The women of the Italian popular novel, in a volume Eco co-wrote: Invernizio's kissed-and-abandoned heroines, Serao's Naples, Liala's aviators. Eco's interest in the consolatory novel did not stop at the border of good taste.

source.label: Biblioteca Universitaria di Bologna, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Peter Haining, The Sherlock Holmes Scrapbook
stops.caption: Fifty years of Holmesiana, as its subtitle has it. Eco read Conan Doyle as a semiotician: his essay on Holmes's method of inference, written with Thomas Sebeok's circle, treats the detective as a philosopher of signs, and William of Baskerville owes him his name.

source.label: Biblioteca Universitaria di Bologna, the record of Eco's copy

image.credit: Sidney Paget (1860-1908), 1903, for The Strand Magazine
image.alt: Holmes and Watson by Sidney Paget, The Strand Magazine (1903)

stops.title: Pierre Bayard, Il caso del mastino dei Baskerville
stops.caption: A French critic reopens The Hound of the Baskervilles and proves Holmes got the wrong murderer. Eco, who put a Baskerville into his own first novel, shelved it in the study.

source.label: Biblioteca Universitaria di Bologna, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Il caso Bond (1965)
stops.caption: The James Bond case: Eco's structural analysis of the Fleming plot, the nine moves every Bond novel makes, published in this collection he edited with Oreste del Buono. He was still bringing it up at dinner forty years later.

source.label: Umberto Eco, 'The Narrative Structure in Fleming' (1965)

stops.title: Ian Fleming, Casino Royale
stops.caption: The first Bond novel, 1953, and the first of the plots Eco took apart: M gives the mission, the villain appears, Bond is captured and tortured, Bond wins, Bond loses the woman.

source.label: Biblioteca Universitaria di Bologna, the record of Eco's copy

stops.title: Umberto Eco, Diario minimo (1963)
stops.caption: Eco's first book of parodies, which includes his praise of Franti, the bad boy of De Amicis's Cuore who laughs at the wrong moments. Eco took the side of the boy who smiled.

source.label: Umberto Eco, 'Elogio di Franti', in Diario minimo (1963)

stops.title: Eroi del racconto popolare
stops.caption: The heroes of popular storytelling, a study shelved among the heroes themselves at the point in the corridor where, Carlotta Eco says, she would begin any account of her father's library.

source.label: Umberto Eco: La biblioteca del mondo (Davide Ferrario, 2022)

quote.text: Se dovessi raccontare la biblioteca di mio padre inizierei da qua: sono i feuilleton, i romanzi d'appendice dell'Ottocento che lui ha letto da ragazzo e che in parte ha letto anche a noi.
quote.attribution: Carlotta Eco, in Davide Ferrario's film Umberto Eco: La biblioteca del mondo (2022)
quote.translation: If I had to tell the story of my father's library I would start from here: these are the feuilletons, the nineteenth-century serial novels that he read as a boy and partly read to us too.
